scenarios.title: The Stolen Laptop
scenarios.situation: An employee's laptop containing customer PII is stolen from a parked car. The drive was fully encrypted with BitLocker and the machine was powered off. The employee asks if the data is safe.
evidence: BitLocker: enabled, AES-256, TPM + PIN protector. Power state at theft: fully off.
choices: The data at rest is protected — without the key the disk is unreadable; still rotate the user's credentials and follow breach-notification policy since device theft is a reportable event
The data is as good as gone — BitLocker only deters casual thieves
No further action is needed — encryption solves the whole incident
BitLocker only protects data while the laptop is powered on
scenarios.why: Full-disk encryption protects data at rest: a powered-off encrypted disk is ciphertext without the key. But encryption does not erase the incident — credentials on the device may be at risk, and most breach-notification regimes still require assessment and reporting. Encryption reduces the blast radius; process handles the rest.
scenarios.hint: What state was the disk in when stolen — powered off, or unlocked and running?

scenarios.title: Pre-Boot Options
scenarios.situation: You are setting the BitLocker standard for executive laptops. Options range from TPM-only (transparent boot) to TPM + PIN + USB startup key.
scenarios.prompt: Which pre-boot configuration is strongest, and what is the trade-off?
choices: TPM + PIN + startup key — multi-factor pre-boot authentication; strongest against theft, at the cost of user inconvenience and PIN/startup-key management overhead
TPM-only — PINs annoy executives and add no real security
No pre-boot authentication — BitLocker alone is sufficient
PIN written on a sticky note under the keyboard — usability first
scenarios.why: TPM-only unlocks transparently: anyone holding the powered-off machine gets a booting OS, and protections rest on the OS login alone. Adding a PIN (something you know) and a startup key (something you have) makes the disk unopenable without those factors — the correct choice for high-value targets, accepting the support overhead of PIN resets and key management.
scenarios.hint: Which option requires something the thief doesn't have — and can't easily take?

scenarios.title: Where's the Recovery Key?
scenarios.situation: An audit finds that the IT team stores BitLocker recovery keys in a spreadsheet — saved on a BitLocker-encrypted file share. 'It's encrypted, so it's safe,' the admin says.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with this picture?
evidence: Recovery keys: single Excel file on encrypted share. Access: 14 IT staff. Backup: none separate from the share.
choices: Recovery keys must be escrowed in a separate secure system (Active Directory, MDM, or a vault) — a key stored on a volume it unlocks is unreachable exactly when you need it, and a shared spreadsheet has no access control or audit trail
Nothing — the share is encrypted, so the keys are protected
Email the keys to each user for safekeeping instead
Use one shared recovery key for all laptops — simpler to manage
scenarios.why: Key management fails in two ways here: availability (if the encrypted share is the thing that's locked, the keys are behind the very lock they open) and control (a spreadsheet shared with 14 people is unaudited, unrevocable access to every disk). Proper escrow separates the keys from the protected volumes, restricts access, and logs every retrieval.
scenarios.hint: When do you need the recovery key — before or after you can unlock the drive?

scenarios.title: Two Admins, One Disk
scenarios.situation: A LUKS-encrypted Linux laptop is shared by two administrators who both know the single passphrase. One of them is leaving the team next month.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct key management move?
evidence: Key slot 0: occupied (shared passphrase). Slots 1-7: free.
choices: Add a second LUKS key slot with an individual passphrase for each admin, then revoke the departing admin's slot — individual credentials enable clean revocation without sharing
Keep sharing one passphrase — the team trusts each other
LUKS only supports one passphrase per disk — nothing to do
Remove encryption — key management is too complex
scenarios.why: LUKS supports up to eight key slots precisely for this: each person gets their own passphrase, and departures mean revoking one slot, not an emergency re-encryption and a new shared secret whispered around. Shared credentials destroy accountability and make every personnel change a cryptographic incident.
scenarios.hint: What happens to a shared secret when one of the sharers leaves?

scenarios.title: Encryption's Blind Spot
scenarios.situation: A BitLocker-protected laptop sits running and unlocked at a desk while its owner gets coffee. An attacker gains two minutes of physical access and plugs in a malicious USB device.
scenarios.prompt: What does this scenario teach about FDE's limits?
evidence: BitLocker: enabled. Power state: running, user logged in, screen unlocked.
choices: FDE protects data at rest, not a running unlocked system — enforce short screen-lock timeouts, idle auto-lock, and DMA protections (Kernel DMA Protection / disable Thunderbolt pre-boot); encryption is not a runtime defense
BitLocker stops all physical attacks regardless of power state
Rebooting the laptop after the incident fully remediates it
FDE is useless — disable it and rely on passwords
scenarios.why: Encryption's guarantee ends the moment the key is in memory and the OS is running: DMA attacks, malicious USB devices, and simple shoulder-surfing all operate above the disk layer. Defense in depth covers the gap — screen locks shrink the window, Kernel DMA Protection blocks malicious PCIe/Thunderbolt devices, and Secure Boot ensures the running OS is the intended one. FDE is one layer, not the whole stack.
scenarios.hint: Encryption protects the disk — what protects the running operating system?

scenarios.title: The USB Dilemma
scenarios.situation: Security wants all removable media blocked; operations says staff need USB drives for field work with no network access. A blanket ban was tried last year and staff simply used personal drives.
scenarios.prompt: What is the balanced, enforceable control?
evidence: Policy: all USB blocked. Reality: 40% of field staff used personal drives (survey). Incidents: 2 malware introductions via personal USB.
choices: Allow only centrally-managed, hardware-encrypted removable media with DLP scanning and usage auditing — a workable policy beats a bypassed ban
Block all USB — policy is policy, regardless of bypasses
Allow all USB drives — convenience comes first
Encrypted USB is pointless — attackers break it anyway
scenarios.why: An unenforceable ban is worse than no policy: it drives behavior underground where you have zero visibility, as last year's personal-drive usage proved. Managed encrypted media gives staff a legitimate path while preserving control — encryption for loss/theft, central management for revocation, and auditing for accountability. Security controls must survive contact with real workflows.
scenarios.hint: What do users do when policy makes their work impossible?

Restart all components — Full-Disk Encryption & Endpoint Hardening issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Full-Disk Encryption & Endpoint Hardening is too complex to troubleshoot systematically

Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

scenarios.title: Where Does the Key Live?
scenarios.situation: A department bought 200 laptops, enabled FDE with a single shared USB startup key 'for convenience,' and stored a copy of the key on a file share 'so nobody gets locked out.' The CISO just learned about it.
choices: The file share needs better permissions — restrict it to IT
The key lifecycle is broken at every stage: shared keys cannot be revoked per-user, the file share is uncontrolled escrow, and there is no rotation or destruction path — the encryption is theater
200 laptops is too many for one department — reduce the fleet
The USB key could be lost — they should buy more USB keys
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. This is not a permissions tweak — it is a lifecycle collapse: a shared key means revoking one person's access revokes everyone's (so nobody ever revokes), the file share is escrow without controls or audit, and no rotation plan exists. The ciphertext is mathematically sound and operationally meaningless. The fix is per-device keys in real escrow with revocation, rotation, and destruction — the system, not the algorithm.
scenarios.hint: If one employee leaves angry tomorrow, what exactly would you revoke — and how long would it take?
objectives: Design key lifecycle before deploying encryption
Treat shared keys as no keys
Escrow without controls is just exposure
evidence: 200 laptops, one shared USB startup key
key copy on a general file share

scenarios.title: The Unlocked Laptop
scenarios.situation: An executive's laptop was stolen from a hotel lobby — powered on, logged in, screen unlocked. The fleet is fully BitLocker-encrypted with TPM+PIN. The executive asks: 'But the disk is encrypted, right?'
choices: No — FDE decrypted the data at boot and the running OS serves files to anyone at the keyboard; the thief has full access. The control that mattered here was auto-lock, not encryption
Partially — the thief can read files but cannot copy them
Only if the thief reboots — then the PIN stops them
Yes — BitLocker protects the disk regardless of power state
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. FDE's promise covers data at rest — powered off or locked. A running, authenticated machine has already decrypted everything by design; the OS will happily serve files to whoever sits down. This is the data-in-use gap, and the honest answer names it: encryption did its job, and it was never the job that mattered here. Auto-lock timers, presence detection, and user training are the controls for this state.
scenarios.hint: At the moment of theft, was the data at rest, in transit, or in use — and which control guards that state?

scenarios.title: The Backup Gap
scenarios.situation: The fleet is 100% FDE-encrypted. Backups run nightly to a NAS — unencrypted, 'because the source disks are encrypted.' An attacker breaches the NAS and exfiltrates the backup images.
choices: Nothing — the backups inherit the source encryption
The backup software — it should have warned about plaintext targets
The data-state map: backups are data at rest in a new location, and they were never encrypted — the FDE boundary ended at the laptop, but the data flowed past it every night
The NAS vendor — their product should encrypt by default
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Encryption boundaries do not travel with data automatically — every place data lands is a new at-rest state needing its own control. The team mapped encryption to devices, not to data flows, so the nightly backup quietly created a plaintext copy of the entire 'encrypted' fleet. The fix is encrypted backup targets (or client-side backup encryption) plus a data-flow map reviewed whenever flows change.
scenarios.hint: Where does the data go after it leaves the encrypted disk — and who encrypted it there?
objectives: Map encryption to data flows, not devices
Treat every new location as a new at-rest state
Review the map when flows change

scenarios.title: The Revocation That Wasn't
scenarios.situation: A sysadmin with BitLocker recovery-key access was terminated Friday. HR collected the laptop; IT disabled the domain account Monday. The recovery keys live in Active Directory, readable by the 'Helpdesk' group the admin belonged to. It is now Wednesday.
choices: Only if they kept the laptop — HR collected it, so fine
None — the domain account is disabled, so access is gone
Low — they would need physical access to a laptop too

Real and ongoing: recovery keys are data, not sessions — the ex-admin could have copied them anytime before Friday, and nothing revoked the keys themselves. Rotate exposed escrow material and audit retrieval logs
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Disabling an account revokes future authentication, not data already copied — recovery keys are static secrets, and a privileged insider had years of opportunity to copy them. The system failure is treating key access as session access: keys need rotation on privileged departure, retrieval logging to detect past abuse, and ideally per-key access controls. 'They can't log in anymore' is true and irrelevant.
scenarios.hint: What did disabling the account actually revoke — and what did it leave untouched?
objectives: Treat keys as copyable data, not sessions
Rotate escrow material on privileged departure
Log key retrieval, not just key storage
evidence: sysadmin terminated Friday, account disabled Monday
AD recovery keys readable by their old group

scenarios.title: Choose the KDF
scenarios.situation: You're specifying password-to-key derivation for a new FDE deployment. Options: raw SHA-256, PBKDF2, Argon2id.
scenarios.prompt: What do you specify and why?
choices: Argon2id with unique 128-bit salts: memory-hardness defeats GPU/ASIC guessing farms that shred PBKDF2/bcrypt; raw SHA-256 is catastrophically fast for attackers — the KDF's slowness IS the security
Raw SHA-256 — fastest for users
PBKDF2 with 1000 iterations — good enough
No KDF — encrypt with the password directly
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. KDF selection is attacker-economics: Argon2id's memory-hardness raises the attacker's cost per guess by orders of magnitude vs PBKDF2, and raw hashes fall in seconds to GPUs. Unique salts kill rainbow tables. The KDF is the password's only armor — specify the strongest practical one.
scenarios.hint: What does the attacker's hardware do to each option's guesses-per-second?

scenarios.title: Scope the Promise
scenarios.situation: Leadership wants to claim 'our laptops are unhackable with FDE.' You're asked to approve the messaging.
choices: Refuse the claim and scope honestly: FDE defeats powered-off theft/loss — it does not stop evil-maid, cold-boot, or running-system attacks; approve 'protects data if devices are lost or stolen while powered off' with the threat matrix attached
Approve — FDE is military-grade
Approve with 'unhackable*' and fine print
Stay silent — not your department
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Overclaiming encryption is a professional integrity issue and a liability: when the inevitable exception occurs (evil maid, compelled disclosure), the 'unhackable' claim becomes the scandal. Precise scoping ('powered-off device theft') is both honest and defensible.
scenarios.hint: What adversary does FDE actually defeat — and which does it not?

scenarios.title: Answer the Auditor
scenarios.situation: HIPAA auditor: 'Encryption is addressable — show me your implementation, alternative, or risk acceptance for §164.312(a)(2)(iv).'
choices: Implementation evidence: FDE deployment report (coverage %), key management documentation, written policy — 'addressable' requires one of the three, and auditors expect implementation; documented deployment with metrics is the answer
'Addressable means optional' — decline to answer
A vendor brochure claiming encryption
Promise to implement next year
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. 'Addressable' is the most misread word in HIPAA: it requires implementation, an equivalent alternative, or documented risk acceptance — and auditors treat missing encryption as a finding. Evidence (coverage reports, key management docs, policy) is what 'implementation' means in an audit.
scenarios.hint: What are the three addressable options — and which do auditors expect?

scenarios.title: Claim the Safe Harbor
scenarios.situation: A laptop with FDE is stolen. Legal asks if breach notification is required.
choices: Likely exempt under most breach-notification safe harbors IF: FDE was active with strong auth at theft time, keys weren't compromised, and you can evidence it — document the encryption state, key status, and timeline for counsel; the safe harbor is the business case for FDE
Always notify — safe harbors don't exist
Never notify — encryption solves everything
Wipe the laptop remotely and stay silent
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Breach safe harbors (state laws, HIPAA) typically exempt properly encrypted data — but 'properly' has conditions: active encryption, uncompromised keys, evidence. The analysis is legal (counsel decides), but the technical inputs (encryption state proof, key status) are yours to provide.
scenarios.hint: What facts does counsel need to claim the safe harbor?

scenarios.title: Explain the Mode
scenarios.situation: An engineer asks why FDE uses XTS instead of CBC mode.
choices: Disks need random access: CBC chains blocks (changing one sector requires re-chaining), while XTS is tweakable — each sector encrypts independently with its position as tweak, enabling random read/write without chaining; ECB would leak patterns, CBC can't random-access efficiently
XTS is faster
CBC is broken
Modes don't matter for disks
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Storage encryption has unique requirements: random-access read/write at sector granularity. XTS's tweak (sector position) gives each sector independent encryption without chaining — CBC's chaining breaks random access, ECB's determinism leaks patterns. Mode selection follows the access pattern.
scenarios.hint: What does a disk do that a network stream doesn't?
objectives: Explain XTS vs CBC vs ECB

scenarios.title: The Quantum Question
scenarios.situation: A board member read that quantum computers will 'break all encryption' and asks whether the AES-256 FDE deployment is now worthless. The CISO needs a two-minute answer.
choices: Nobody knows — say quantum is hype and move on
Double all key lengths just in case
Yes — start ripping out AES-256 immediately

No: quantum computers threaten asymmetric crypto (RSA/ECC key exchange) via Shor's algorithm; symmetric AES-256 is only weakened (Grover's halves effective strength to ~128 bits, still strong). The FDE deployment stands — the migration to watch is post-quantum key exchange, tracked via your algorithm inventory
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Precision matters: Shor's algorithm breaks RSA/ECC (key exchange, signatures), Grover's only quadratically weakens symmetric ciphers — AES-256 retains ~128-bit post-quantum strength, which remains secure. Ripping out FDE (C) would destroy real protection over a misunderstood threat; dismissal (A) ignores the genuine asymmetric migration ahead. The action item is crypto-agility: inventory algorithms now so the PQC transition is planned.
scenarios.hint: Which algorithms does quantum actually break — and is AES-256 one of them?
objectives: Keep AES-256, plan PQC for asymmetric

domains.name: BitLocker: Enterprise Windows Encryption

scenarios.title: Stack the Protectors
scenarios.situation: CISO: 'Our executives travel with sensitive data. TPM-only BitLocker is deployed. Is that enough?'
choices: No — upgrade to TPM+PIN: TPM-only has no pre-boot human authentication, so a stolen laptop's TPM will happily unseal for anyone who powers it on; add PIN (6+ digits), enforce escrow, and enable Network Unlock for office convenience
Yes — TPM is hardware security, that's enough
Remove BitLocker — it slows boot
TPM-only is fine for executives
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. TPM-only binds to boot integrity, not to user identity — it stops boot-tampering, not theft. TPM+PIN adds the human factor that makes stolen laptops actually resistant. The executive threat model (targeted theft) demands it; Network Unlock preserves office convenience.
scenarios.hint: What does the TPM authenticate — the boot chain or the human?

scenarios.title: Handle the Airport Call
scenarios.situation: Executive at an airport: BitLocker recovery screen, flight in 40 minutes, no access to internal network.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct helpdesk flow?
choices: Verify identity per policy (callback, MFA), retrieve escrowed 48-digit key, read it group-by-group with readback, unlock — then schedule post-recovery investigation; speed matters but identity verification is non-negotiable
Read the key immediately — flights matter most
Tell them to wait until they're back in the office
Give them the key without verification — it's urgent
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Recovery is a security event: social engineers specifically target 'urgent BitLocker recovery' scenarios. Identity verification (callback to known number, MFA) precedes key release; group-by-group readback prevents typos under pressure. Urgency doesn't waive verification.
scenarios.hint: What would an attacker do with this exact pretext?

scenarios.title: Explain the Recovery Wave
scenarios.situation: After a firmware update, 300 machines drop to BitLocker recovery simultaneously. Helpdesk is drowning.
scenarios.prompt: What happened and what is the fix?
choices: PCR drift: the firmware update changed measured boot components, invalidating sealed keys — expected behavior; suspend BitLocker before firmware updates fleet-wide (scripted), then resume after; for the 300, run bulk recovery with escrowed keys
The update broke BitLocker — roll it back
BitLocker is unreliable — disable it
The TPMs are all faulty
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. PCR-bound keys correctly refuse to unseal when boot measurements change — the mechanism working as designed. Fleet procedure: scripted suspend-protection before firmware updates, resume after. The 300 need bulk escrow recovery, then the process fix prevents recurrence.
scenarios.hint: Is this BitLocker failing — or BitLocker working?

scenarios.title: Audit the Escrow
scenarios.situation: Compliance audit: 'Prove every encrypted laptop's recovery key is escrowed.' Your report shows 92% escrowed.
choices: Acknowledge the 8% gap as a finding with a remediation plan: identify the unescrowed devices (policy exceptions? failed escrow?), force escrow or re-provision, and implement continuous escrow verification — 92% is a failing grade for recoverability
92% is good enough — report it as compliant
Hide the 8% — auditors won't dig
Escrow doesn't matter if encryption works
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Unescrowed encryption is unrecoverable encryption — the 8% represents guaranteed data loss on PIN failure. Auditors test escrow specifically because it's the recoverability control. The professional response: own the gap, remediate devices, and implement continuous verification so it never recurs.
scenarios.hint: What happens to the 8% when their users forget PINs?

scenarios.title: Stage the Rollout
scenarios.situation: You're deploying BitLocker to 5,000 machines. Leadership wants it all next weekend.
scenarios.prompt: What is the professional rollout plan?
choices: Staged: pilot IT (50) → validate GPO/escrow/reporting → executives/high-risk → phased departments over 6-8 weeks, with escrow verification and helpdesk recovery drills throughout — big-bang encryption at scale turns policy bugs into fleet-wide data-loss events
Do it all next weekend — leadership wants speed
Deploy silently without telling users
Encrypt only new machines going forward
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Encryption rollouts fail at scale when policy is wrong: unescrowed keys, PIN confusion, recovery storms. Staged rollout contains each failure mode to a manageable cohort while validating the machinery. The pilot's job is finding the bugs; the phases' job is limiting blast radius.
scenarios.hint: What breaks at 5,000 machines that works fine at 50?

scenarios.title: The Suspended Protector
scenarios.situation: A technician 'temporarily' suspended BitLocker protection to image a drive for a software deployment — 6 weeks ago, on 45 machines. The protectors were never re-enabled. A laptop from that batch is now missing.
scenarios.prompt: What is the exposure and the fix?
choices: Low — suspension is temporary by design and re-enables itself

High: suspended protection means the volume master key is stored unsealed — those 45 disks are effectively unencrypted to anyone with physical access. Re-enable protectors fleet-wide immediately, verify via telemetry, and treat the missing laptop as unencrypted in the incident classification
Re-image the 45 machines to fix it
Only the missing laptop matters — handle that one
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Suspended BitLocker writes the clear key to disk — by design, for reboots during maintenance — and 'temporary' without a re-enable step is permanent exposure. All 45 machines need protectors re-enabled and verified; the missing laptop must be classified as unencrypted (breach-class per its data). Re-imaging (C) is unnecessary surgery; scoping to one laptop (D) ignores 44 identical exposures.
scenarios.hint: What does 'suspended' actually do to the volume master key — and for how long has it been that way?
evidence: one laptop from batch now missing
