domains.name: LUKS: Linux Disk Encryption

scenarios.title: Revoke the Departed
scenarios.situation: An admin with LUKS passphrase knowledge leaves abruptly. The volumes use single-slot passphrases.
choices: Emergency rotation via key slots: add new slot with new credential → verify unlock → revoke the departed admin's slot → update escrow — no re-encryption needed, thanks to slot architecture; then fix the process (per-admin slots going forward)
Re-encrypt all volumes — the only safe path
Change nothing — they wouldn't abuse it
Delete their user account — sufficient
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. LUKS key slots make this a 10-minute operation: add-verify-revoke, no re-encryption. The incident also exposes the process failure — shared single slots can't be revoked per-person. Going forward: per-admin slots, so departures mean revoking one slot.
scenarios.hint: What does the slot architecture make cheap that re-encryption makes expensive?

scenarios.title: Unlock the Dark Server
scenarios.situation: A colo server with LUKS reboots at 3 AM. No console access. It's waiting at the passphrase prompt.
choices: Remote unlock: Dropbear SSH in initramfs (unlock via SSH) or TPM2+Clevis/NetworkBoundDisk for trusted-boot auto-unlock — headless FDE without remote unlock guarantees 3 AM datacenter trips
Remove encryption from servers — too inconvenient
Leave the passphrase on a sticky note in the rack
Disable reboots
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Headless + FDE requires an unlock path: Dropbear SSH (manual remote entry) or TPM2-bound auto-unlock (for trusted environments). Deploying FDE without solving the unlock problem just moves the outage from 'data exposed' to 'server down at 3 AM.'
scenarios.hint: Who types the passphrase at 3 AM with no console?

scenarios.title: Save the Header
scenarios.situation: A LUKS volume won't unlock — 'no key slot' errors. The header region has bad sectors. No backup exists.
scenarios.prompt: What is the prognosis and lesson?
choices: Data almost certainly lost: the header holds all key slots; without a backup, damaged headers are cryptographically unrecoverable — the lesson is mandatory header backups (luksHeaderBackup) stored separately, tested by restore
Try more passphrases — one will work
The data is still there — carve it with photorec
Reinstall the OS — it'll fix the header
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Encrypted data without its header is random noise — carving can't help, passphrases can't help. The header is the single point of failure, which is exactly why backups are mandatory and must be tested. This incident is the training story for the whole team.
scenarios.hint: What does the passphrase unlock without the header?

scenarios.title: Decommission Securely
scenarios.situation: Retiring 50 LUKS-encrypted drives. The recycler wants them intact for resale value.
choices: Cryptographic erase: cryptsetup erase wipes all key slots — data becomes unrecoverable without re-encrypting; document the erasure per drive; resale-safe and instant vs multi-hour overwrites
Quick format — good enough
Sell as-is — they're encrypted
Physical destruction only — no resale
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Crypto-erase (slot wiping) is the elegant decommission: destroying key material renders ciphertext permanently unreadable in seconds, preserving resale value. 'Encrypted, so sell as-is' gambles on slot hygiene; physical destruction wastes value. Document per-drive for the audit trail.
scenarios.hint: What makes the ciphertext unreadable — and how long does it take?

scenarios.title: Layer It Right
scenarios.situation: New Linux deployment: separate /, /home, swap. The admin encrypted each LV with its own passphrase.
choices: LUKS on the PV, LVM inside: one LUKS container encrypts the physical volume; all LVs (/, /home, swap) live inside unlocked together — one passphrase, everything (including swap) encrypted, single key management
Current setup is fine — more passphrases, more security
Encrypt only /home — that's where data lives
Skip swap encryption — it's temporary
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. LUKS-on-PV with LVM inside is the standard: one unlock opens everything, swap included (memory contents page to swap — unencrypted swap leaks keys). Per-LV passphrases multiply management burden without adding security. Architecture matters more than passphrase count.
scenarios.hint: Where does swap fit — and what lives in it?

scenarios.title: The Passphrase Policy
scenarios.situation: Your Linux fleet uses LUKS with user-chosen passphrases. An audit finds passphrases like 'password123' and 'company2024' on 30% of machines. The security team proposes mandatory 32-character random passphrases.
choices: Enforce 32-character random passphrases — security first, usability second

Adopt a balanced policy: LUKS with a strong passphrase OR (better) TPM-backed sealing plus a shorter PIN — because unusable security gets bypassed; pair the policy with key-slot hygiene (revoke departed users' slots) and escrow of recovery keys
Keep user passphrases — training will fix it
Remove LUKS and rely on physical security
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Thirty-two-character mandates produce sticky notes, not security — the workable design reduces the human burden (TPM sealing + PIN) while keeping strength, and fixes the real gaps: stale key slots for departed users and missing escrow. Mandates (A) optimize for audit checkboxes over actual behavior; training alone (C) has already failed; removing LUKS (D) surrenders the control.
scenarios.hint: Will users actually follow the policy — and what happens when they don't?
objectives: Fix key slots and escrow alongside policy

domains.summary: LUKS architecture, deployment, key management, forensics — the Linux standard.

domains.name: TPM and Secure Boot

scenarios.title: Seal to the Right PCRs
scenarios.situation: You're sealing disk-encryption keys to PCRs. The vendor suggests PCRs 0-7 (all firmware measurements).
choices: Over-binding: firmware updates change PCRs 0-7 frequently, causing recovery storms on every update — balance tamper detection (enough PCRs) against operational stability (not every PCR); 0,2,4,11 is the common compromise
More PCRs is always better — accept it
PCRs don't matter — skip sealing
Bind to PCR 23 only — simplest
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. PCR selection is a stability/security trade: binding everything detects all tampering but breaks on every legitimate update; binding too little misses attacks. The standard sets (0,2,4,11) reflect hard-won operational experience — tamper-evident where it counts, stable across updates.
scenarios.hint: What changes PCRs more often — attackers or firmware updates?

scenarios.title: Clear Carefully
scenarios.situation: A motherboard is being replaced under warranty. The TPM holds sealed BitLocker keys.
choices: Suspend protection (or capture recovery key), replace board, clear TPM on the new board, re-provision and re-seal — the old TPM's sealed data dies with the board; the recovery key bridges the transition
Just swap the board — TPMs transfer
Clear the TPM before capturing the recovery key
Skip BitLocker during the swap
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. TPMs are bound to their motherboard — sealed keys don't migrate. The sequence (suspend/capture → swap → clear → re-provision) preserves data through the transition. Clearing before capturing the key is the catastrophic order.
scenarios.hint: What happens to sealed data when the TPM is replaced?

scenarios.title: Gate the Network
scenarios.situation: You want unhealthy machines (wrong OS build) blocked from the VPN automatically.
choices: TPM remote attestation: clients quote PCRs to a verifier; the verifier compares against approved baselines; VPN grants access only on match — hardware-proven compliance, not self-reported
Ask users to confirm they're updated
Block by IP range
Annual manual audits
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Attestation moves compliance from self-report to hardware proof: the TPM signs the boot measurements, the verifier checks them against policy. Unhealthy machines fail closed automatically. Self-attestation is theater; hardware attestation is enforcement.
scenarios.hint: Who do you trust for the health report — the OS or the TPM?

scenarios.title: Update TPM Firmware
scenarios.situation: A TPM firmware vulnerability is announced. 2000 machines affected. The update clears TPM state.
choices: Staged with key backup: verify escrow coverage first (no key loss), pilot the update (confirm re-provisioning works), then phase the fleet — firmware updates that clear TPMs without escrow verification cause mass data loss
Push to all 2000 immediately — security first
Ignore it — TPM vulnerabilities are theoretical
Disable TPMs to avoid the issue
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. TPM firmware updates that clear state are key-destruction events without escrow — the update plan is really a key-safety plan with a firmware step. Escrow verification first, pilot second, phases third. 'Security first' without key safety is data-loss first.
scenarios.hint: What does the update destroy — and what must exist before it runs?

scenarios.title: Retire the 1.2s
scenarios.situation: Inventory finds 300 TPM 1.2 machines in a 5000-device fleet. They're working fine.
choices: Planned retirement: 1.2 lacks 2.0's algorithm agility and security properties; include them in the refresh cycle with priority by data sensitivity — 'working' isn't 'adequate' for hardware roots of trust
Leave them — they work
Disable their TPMs to standardize on no-TPM
Replace all 300 tomorrow
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Hardware roots of trust age: 1.2's fixed algorithms and weaker properties make it technical debt, not a working solution. Planned, prioritized retirement (sensitive data first) beats both neglect and panic replacement.
scenarios.hint: What's the difference between working and adequate for a root of trust?

scenarios.title: The PCR Mismatch After Update
scenarios.situation: A fleet-wide firmware update changes PCR measurements. Monday morning, 600 laptops drop into BitLocker recovery — keys sealed to the old PCR values no longer unseal. The helpdesk is overwhelmed.
scenarios.prompt: What is the immediate fix and the systemic lesson?
choices: Disable TPM sealing permanently — too fragile for production

Immediate: use escrowed recovery keys to unlock and re-seal to new PCRs (scripted, prioritized by VIP/critical). Systemic: firmware updates must include a PCR re-sealing step in the deployment runbook, tested in pilot rings before fleet-wide rollout
Tell users to enter recovery keys themselves from the escrow portal
Roll back the firmware update
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. PCR-sealed keys are supposed to fail closed on firmware change — that is the security property working. The failure was operational: the update runbook lacked the re-seal step and pilot validation. Self-service (C) at this scale is chaos; rollback (D) may be impossible and abandons the security fix; disabling sealing (A) trades the protection for convenience permanently. Script the recovery, fix the runbook.
scenarios.hint: Did the TPM fail — or did it do exactly what sealing promises, while the runbook failed?
objectives: Pilot firmware updates before fleet rollout
Script mass recovery, don't improvise it
evidence: PCR values changed; keys sealed to old measurements

domains.summary: Hardware roots of trust: TPM capabilities, PCRs, Secure Boot chains — the silicon beneath encryption.

domains.name: Key Management and Escrow

scenarios.title: Prove the Escrow
scenarios.situation: CISO: 'Show me that every encrypted device's keys are recoverable.' You have deployment reports but no retrieval tests.
choices: Honest gap + remediation: deployment ≠ recoverability — run a retrieval drill (sample devices, actual key recovery), report the results, and implement quarterly drills; untested escrow is a claim, not a control
Show the deployment report — 100% deployed means recoverable
Claim it's fine — no incidents yet
Blame the tool vendor
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The distinction that matters: deployed encryption vs proven recoverability. Retrieval drills convert the claim into evidence. 'No incidents yet' is luck, not control. The CISO asked the right question — answer it with a test, not a report.
scenarios.hint: What's the difference between deployed and recoverable?

scenarios.title: Rotate on Departure
scenarios.situation: A key administrator leaves. They knew the escrow vault credentials and several volume passwords.
choices: Full rotation: vault credentials, affected volume credentials (via slot/PIN rotation — no re-encryption where architecture allows), and access reviews — the departure of a key-holder is a compromise-equivalent event for the keys they knew
Just disable their account
Nothing — they signed an NDA
Rotate everything including DEKs with full re-encryption
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Key-holders' departures are key-compromise events for every key they knew — NDAs don't un-know credentials. Rotation scope covers all known credentials, using cheap operations (slot rotation, PIN changes) where the architecture allows. Disabling accounts doesn't un-know passwords.
scenarios.hint: What does the departed admin still know — and what does that imply?

scenarios.title: Justify the HSM
scenarios.situation: You're asked to approve HSMs for all application keys. Cost: $200k + operational overhead.
choices: Tier by key value: HSMs for Tier-1 (CA keys, master escrow) where compromise is catastrophic; cloud KMS for application keys (HSM-backed, fractional cost); software vaults for operational secrets — $200k for everything is un-tiered spending
Approve — HSMs for everything is safest
Reject — HSMs are never worth it
Approve the cheapest HSM option
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Key protection should be proportional to key value — tiering (HSM/cloud-KMS/vault) gets hardware-grade protection where it matters at sustainable cost. Blanket HSM deployment wastes budget that could fund other controls; blanket rejection leaves crown jewels in software.
scenarios.hint: What is each key worth to an attacker — and what protection does that justify?

scenarios.title: Shred It Right
scenarios.situation: Decommissioning: 200 encrypted drives, mixed classifications, auditor watching.
choices: Crypto-shredding with documentation: destroy key material per drive (slot wipe), record serials + method + witnesses per NIST 800-88, issue certificates of sanitization — seconds per drive, auditable, resale-preserving
Quick-format them all
Drill holes in all 200
Stack them in a closet — they're encrypted
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Crypto-shredding (key destruction) is NIST-recognized sanitization for encrypted media — fast, effective, documented. Two-person integrity and per-drive records satisfy the auditor. Physical destruction wastes resale value; quick-format isn't sanitization; closet storage isn't disposition.
scenarios.hint: What makes ciphertext permanently unreadable — and how do you prove it per drive?

scenarios.title: Gate the Vault
scenarios.situation: Helpdesk requests standing access to the key escrow vault 'for efficiency.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct access model?
choices: Ticketed break-glass: no standing access — retrieval requires an approved ticket, MFA, time-bounded elevation, and full audit logging; efficiency doesn't justify persistent access to the keys of the kingdom
Grant it — helpdesk needs speed
Grant read-only standing access
Let the helpdesk manager decide per case
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Escrow access is the highest-privilege operation in the encryption program — standing access creates a persistent high-value target. Break-glass (ticketed, MFA, time-bounded, logged) balances emergency speed with security. 'Efficiency' is how vaults get compromised.
scenarios.hint: What's the blast radius of a compromised always-on vault credential?

scenarios.title: The Single Custodian
scenarios.situation: All HSM admin credentials are held by one engineer — 'the crypto person.' They are going on a 3-week remote trek with no connectivity. An HSM firmware update is scheduled during week 2.
scenarios.prompt: What is the risk and the fix?
choices: Critical single-point-of-failure: establish dual custodianship now (split credentials/roles between two trained admins), defer or reassign the firmware update, and document the ceremony — one person holding all key infrastructure is an outage and a compromise waiting to happen
Cancel their vacation — business need
Give the credentials to the helpdesk temporarily
No risk — the HSM runs itself for 3 weeks
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Single-custodian key infrastructure fails on vacation, illness, resignation — and concentrates compromise risk in one person. Dual control (two custodians, split knowledge) is the standard for a reason; the firmware update gets deferred or done by the second custodian. Canceling leave (B) is unsustainable; helpdesk handoff (C) explodes the trust boundary.
scenarios.hint: What happens if that one person is unreachable during an HSM emergency — who acts?

domains.summary: The discipline that decides whether encryption is recoverable or a data-loss program: escrow, rotation, and lifecycle.

domains.name: Mobile and Removable Media

scenarios.title: Seize the State
scenarios.situation: A phone is seized while unlocked (AFU). It's encrypted with a strong passcode. How worried are you?
scenarios.prompt: How worried should you be, and why?
choices: Significantly: AFU keeps class keys in memory — forensic tools exploit the unlocked state; BFU (rebooted, never unlocked) would be far more resistant — the seizure state, not just the encryption, determines the outcome
Not worried — encryption is encryption
Wipe it remotely — problem solved
The passcode strength is all that matters
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Mobile encryption's strength is state-dependent: BFU evicts keys (strong), AFU retains them for functionality (weaker against forensic tools). Remote wipe needs connectivity and races the examiner. High-risk users should understand: reboot before risky crossings.
scenarios.hint: What keys are in memory in AFU vs BFU?

scenarios.title: Close the USB Gap
scenarios.situation: DLP alerts: large transfers to unencrypted personal USB drives, weekly. Policy prohibits it.
choices: Technical enforcement: DLP agent blocks unencrypted USB (allow only hardware-encrypted or BitLocker To Go volumes), alerts on attempts — policy documents don't stop transfers; endpoint enforcement does
Send a reminder email about the policy
Discipline one employee publicly
Ban all USB — including encrypted
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The weekly pattern proves policy-only fails — enforcement must be technical (DLP blocking unencrypted media) with graduated response (encrypted allowed, unencrypted blocked, attempts logged). Blanket bans punish legitimate use; reminders change nothing.
scenarios.hint: What actually stops the next transfer — the policy or the agent?

scenarios.title: Check the Backup
scenarios.situation: Fleet phones are encrypted and MDM-managed. Backups go to a consumer cloud service, unencrypted.
choices: Backup bypass: the encrypted device's data sits plaintext in the cloud — attackers target the weaker backup; enforce encrypted backups (platform backup encryption + MDM policy) — the chain is only as strong as its cloud link
No gap — the phones are encrypted
Backups don't matter
Ban backups entirely
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Encryption scope must include backups — an encrypted phone with plaintext cloud backup just moves the target. Platform backup encryption (iTunes encrypted backups, Android backup encryption) plus MDM enforcement closes it. Threat models that stop at the device miss the cloud.
scenarios.hint: Where does the data rest besides the phone?

scenarios.title: Verify the Wipe
scenarios.situation: A lost executive phone: MDM wipe issued, but the device is offline. What's the exposure?
choices: Wipe pending: offline devices can't receive the command — exposure lasts until connectivity; mitigations: strong passcode + BFU maximizes resistance meanwhile; verify wipe acknowledgment when it reconnects; treat as potentially compromised until confirmed
Wiped — the command was sent
No exposure — MDM handles it
Buy a new phone and move on
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Remote wipe is a queued command, not an executed one — offline devices hold data until they reconnect. The interim defense is device-side (passcode strength, BFU state). Verification of acknowledgment closes the loop; assumption doesn't.
scenarios.hint: What does 'wipe issued' guarantee about an offline device?

scenarios.title: Spot the Rogue Profile
scenarios.situation: Users report installing a 'free VPN' profile that requested traffic interception permissions.
scenarios.prompt: What is the risk and response?
choices: Rogue configuration profile: installed profiles can proxy traffic, install roots, and persist — treat as compromise: remove the profile, rotate credentials used on the device, audit what it could observe, and educate on profile installation risks
Free VPNs are fine — leave it
It's just a VPN — no risk
Wipe all phones preemptively
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Configuration profiles are powerful — traffic interception via installed roots is a full MITM. 'Free VPN' profiles are a classic vector. Response: remove, rotate exposed credentials, assess observation window, and train users that profiles are system-level trust decisions.
scenarios.hint: What can an installed profile do that an app can't?

scenarios.title: The Personal Phone With Company Data
scenarios.situation: A departing sales rep used their personal phone (no MDM, no containerization) for email and CRM for 2 years. They leave Friday. The phone holds customer lists and quoted pricing.
choices: Remote-wipe the personal phone — company data justifies it
None — it's their property, wish them well

Selective wipe of the managed data only works if a container existed — it doesn't. Real options: legal hold letter + attestation of deletion, revoke all tokens/sessions immediately, rotate shared credentials they knew, and fix the policy gap (MDM/container or no company data on personal devices) so this never recurs
Ask them nicely to delete the apps
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Full wipe of a personal device (A) is legally explosive and often unlawful; doing nothing (B) abandons customer data; asking nicely (D) is not a control. The honest answer: without prior containerization, technical options are near zero — so you revoke access (tokens, sessions, credentials), create legal accountability (hold letter, deletion attestation), and close the policy hole that allowed unmanaged personal devices to hold customer data for two years.
scenarios.hint: What technical control exists on that phone today — and what does its absence leave you with?
objectives: Containerize before you need to wipe
evidence: personal phone, no MDM, 2 years of CRM/email

domains.summary: Encryption beyond laptops: phones, USB drives, and the unique challenges of mobile platforms.

domains.name: Digital Forensics Fundamentals

scenarios.title: The Dying Laptop
scenarios.situation: You arrive to seize a suspect's laptop: it is powered on, logged in, BitLocker-encrypted, battery at 8%, no charger in sight. The suspect is being detained in the next room.
choices: Ask the suspect for the password first
Power it down cleanly to preserve the disk state
Photograph the screen, start a RAM capture immediately, and get it on portable power — volatile keys and decrypted state die with the battery
Bag it and transport to the lab — the lab has proper tools
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. At 8% battery, you are minutes from losing the only copy of the decryption keys in RAM — powering down (B) or transporting (D) guarantees that loss, since the encrypted disk is then a brick. RAM capture plus portable power preserves both the keys and the decrypted volume state. Asking for the password (A) wastes the critical minutes and tips off nothing useful yet.
scenarios.hint: What disappears forever when that battery hits zero — and can you get it back?
evidence: on, logged in, BitLocker, 8% battery, no charger

scenarios.title: Whose Key Is It Anyway
scenarios.situation: A powered-off laptop seized from a corporate fraud suspect. IT confirms: BitLocker keys are escrowed in Active Directory, and the suspect's manager can approve retrieval. Legal counsel says the warrant covers the device but is silent on the escrow system.
choices: Image the encrypted disk first (preserving it bit-for-bit), then have counsel clarify escrow coverage before retrieving the key — the image is safe to take, the key retrieval needs clear authority
Ask the suspect nicely and hope for cooperation
Try common passwords — faster than lawyers
Pull the key from AD now — the warrant covers the investigation
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Imaging the ciphertext needs no key and preserves everything immediately — do that now. But the escrow system is a separate system with its own access controls and legal scope; retrieving the key under an ambiguous warrant risks suppression of everything it unlocks. Counsel clarifies coverage (often a quick supplement), then retrieval is clean. Password guessing (C) is unprofessional and potentially altering; relying on cooperation (B) is not a plan.
scenarios.hint: Which action is safe right now, and which one needs counsel's green light first?
objectives: Get clear authority for key retrieval
evidence: off, BitLocker, key in AD escrow

scenarios.title: The Write-Blocker Question
scenarios.situation: A junior analyst imaged a suspect's SSD by connecting it directly via a USB dock — no write-blocker — 'because SSDs don't spin and it was faster.' The image hash was recorded after acquisition. Defense counsel just asked about the acquisition method.
choices: Minor — SSDs cannot be written by just connecting them
Fixable — re-image it properly and discard the first image
None — the hash proves the image is accurate

Potentially fatal: without a write-blocker, the OS may have written to the source (journal updates, timestamps), so the defense can argue the original was altered — and the post-acquisition hash cannot prove otherwise
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Modern OSes write to mounted volumes automatically — journal replays, access-time updates, background indexing — so 'it was faster' likely altered the source. The hash only proves the image matches whatever the source had become by acquisition time, not that the source was pristine. Re-imaging (B) cannot un-ring the bell: the original state is unrecoverable, and the defense now has a documented alteration vector.
scenarios.hint: What does the hash actually prove — and what happened before it was taken?

scenarios.title: Live Capture Disclosure
scenarios.situation: During live triage of a running server, you ran six commands to capture RAM, network state, and process lists. The captures look great. Your report draft describes the findings but not the commands.
scenarios.prompt: What must change before the report goes out?
choices: Nothing — the findings are what matter
Add a methodology section listing every command run, in order, with timestamps — live acquisition alters state, and undisclosed alteration destroys credibility under cross-examination
Re-run everything in a sandbox to avoid mentioning live commands
Summarize the commands vaguely to avoid confusing the jury
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Live forensics inherently alters the system — that is accepted practice, but only when fully disclosed: exact commands, order, timestamps, and the known effects. An undisclosed alteration discovered by the defense (and they will check) converts a professional capture into a credibility crisis. Vague summaries (D) are concealment with better formatting; sandbox re-runs (C) do not describe what actually happened to the evidence.
scenarios.hint: If the defense asks 'what exactly did you type into that server,' what will your answer be?
objectives: Treat alteration as disclosable, not shameful

scenarios.title: The Cloud Backup Shortcut
scenarios.situation: The seized phone is encrypted and locked, no escrow, owner uncooperative. But the suspect's cloud account shows a full device backup from last night — likely unencrypted at rest in the provider's storage, accessible with legal process.
choices: Ask the provider informally for a favor — faster than a warrant
Wipe the phone to trigger a fresh backup
Keep attacking the phone — the device is the real evidence
Pursue legal process for the cloud backup immediately while preserving the phone powered and secured — the backup is likely the fastest path to the data, and the phone stays available for later
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Attack the accessible copy, not the hardened original: cloud backups are frequently the plaintext path around device encryption, and proper legal process makes the results admissible. Preserve the phone in parallel (powered, Faraday) in case the backup is incomplete. Informal favors (A) poison admissibility; wiping (B) destroys evidence; device-only focus (C) ignores the open door.
scenarios.hint: Where is the data easiest to lawfully reach — the hardened device, or its backup?
objectives: Pursue the most accessible lawful copy
Use proper legal process for providers
evidence: encrypted, locked, no escrow, uncooperative owner
full cloud backup last night, legal process available

scenarios.title: Hibernation File Gold
scenarios.situation: A powered-off Windows laptop, BitLocker-encrypted, no escrow key available. But the hibernation file (hiberfil.sys) is on an unencrypted recovery partition — the user disabled BitLocker on that partition 'for faster boot.'
scenarios.prompt: What does the hibernation file potentially contain?
choices: Malware signatures at best
Nothing useful — hibernation files are compressed system state

A full RAM snapshot from the last hibernation, potentially including the BitLocker volume master key or the user's plaintext passphrase — image it through a write-blocker and analyze before assuming the disk is a brick
Only the desktop wallpaper and open window positions
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Hibernation writes RAM contents — including encryption keys and passphrases in memory at hibernate time — to disk. An unencrypted hiberfil.sys is a classic key-recovery vector and exactly why encryption policies must cover all partitions. The 'faster boot' exception created the hole. Image it forensically and search for key material before declaring the evidence inaccessible.
scenarios.hint: What was in RAM the last time that machine hibernated — and where did RAM go?
objectives: Check all partitions, not just the encrypted one
Treat hibernation files as RAM snapshots
Close policy exceptions that leak keys
evidence: BitLocker on OS partition; recovery partition unencrypted

scenarios.title: The Timestamp Trap
scenarios.situation: Your timeline shows the suspect's document was 'created' two days after their arrest — while the laptop sat in your evidence safe. The prosecutor is alarmed; the defense is delighted.
choices: Your analyst opened the file during examination without a write-blocker or on a mounted image, updating access timestamps — an examination artifact, not suspect activity
The system clock was wrong at seizure
The timeline tool is defective — switch tools
The suspect remotely accessed the evidence locker — investigate a breach
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Examination alters metadata: opening files updates access times, mounting read-write updates journals. This is why analysts work on forensic copies through write-blockers and document every access — and why the report must distinguish evidence timestamps from examination artifacts. A breach (D) is possible but the mundane explanation (your own handling) comes first; tool-blaming (C) avoids the real lesson.
scenarios.hint: Who touched that file most recently — the suspect, or your analyst?
evidence: file 'created' 2 days post-arrest, in evidence safe

scenarios.title: Report Language
scenarios.situation: Your draft report says: 'The suspect deleted the files to hide evidence of fraud.' Your supervisor flags the sentence.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with it, and what is the fix?
choices: Nothing — the timestamps prove deletion after the subpoena

It states intent as fact: you can report that files were deleted and when (facts), but 'to hide evidence' is an inference about motive — rewrite as fact plus labeled opinion, and let the court draw conclusions
It is too tentative — experts should be decisive
Delete the sentence entirely — never mention deletions
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Forensic reports separate fact ('12 files deleted 2026-10-03 14:22, after subpoena service') from opinion ('in my opinion, the timing is consistent with concealment') — motive inferences belong to the court, not the examiner. Overstating (A, C) hands the defense a credibility attack; omitting (D) withholds relevant findings. Precision about the fact/opinion line is what makes experts believed.
scenarios.hint: What did you observe — and what did you conclude? Are they the same sentence?
evidence: 'suspect deleted files to hide evidence of fraud'

domains.summary: Evidence handling where encryption is the obstacle.

domains.name: Enterprise Key Escrow

scenarios.title: The Spreadsheet Escrow
scenarios.situation: During an audit you discover a regional IT team has been storing BitLocker recovery keys in a shared spreadsheet 'temporarily' — for 14 months, 340 keys, shared with 22 people including interns.
choices: Treat it as a key-compromise event: inventory which keys were exposed, rotate the affected devices' keys into proper escrow, restrict and log access going forward, and document the remediation for the auditors
Restrict the spreadsheet to the IT team and keep using it — it works
Report the interns but keep the process
Delete the spreadsheet and move on — problem solved
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Twenty-two people had uncontrolled, unaudited access to 340 master keys for over a year — that is a compromise by definition, since you cannot prove non-access. Deleting (D) destroys the evidence of scope without fixing the exposure; restricting (B) legitimizes a broken process; blaming interns (C) misses the systemic failure. Rotate, re-escrow properly, document — then fix the process that allowed it.
scenarios.hint: Can you prove none of those 22 people copied a key — and if not, what does that mean?
objectives: Rotate after exposure, don't just delete
evidence: 340 keys, 22 people, 14 months, no audit trail

scenarios.title: The 3 AM Bulk Retrieval
scenarios.situation: Your SIEM alerts: a helpdesk account retrieved 47 recovery keys between 2:00 and 3:00 AM. The technician says they were 'catching up on tickets.' There is no ticket for 40 of the retrievals.
choices: Remind them to file tickets and move on
Restrict helpdesk retrieval to business hours going forward
Accept the explanation — ticket backlog is real

Disable the account immediately, preserve logs, investigate as a potential compromise: 40 unticketed bulk retrievals at 3 AM is the textbook insider/attacker pattern — then rotate the 47 devices' keys regardless of findings
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Bulk, unticketed, off-hours retrieval is indistinguishable from key harvesting until proven otherwise — treat it as an incident first, an HR matter second. The 47 keys must be rotated because you cannot prove they were not copied; that is non-negotiable regardless of the investigation's outcome. Accepting the story (C) or a reminder (A) leaves potentially-compromised keys in place; hours-restriction (B) is a fine future control but not an incident response.
scenarios.hint: If those keys were harvested, what undoes the damage — and does anything else?

scenarios.title: The Orphaned Admin
scenarios.situation: Quarterly access review finds a domain admin account — owner left 8 months ago — still has read access to the BitLocker recovery-key OU in AD. The account was disabled at departure but re-enabled 'temporarily' for a migration and never re-disabled.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct action set?
choices: Delete the account to prevent future issues
Disable it now and note it in the review — done

Disable immediately, audit what the account accessed while enabled (retrieval logs, if any), rotate keys for any devices whose keys it could have read, and fix the process that allows 'temporary' re-enables without expiry
Leave it — the owner is gone, so nobody is using it
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. An enabled privileged account for a departed employee is an open door — and eight months of potential access means you must assume the keys were readable and check the logs. Rotation of potentially-exposed keys is the containment; the process fix (expiring temporary access) prevents recurrence. Just disabling (B) closes the door without checking what walked through it; deletion (A) destroys the audit trail you need.
scenarios.hint: The account was enabled for 8 months — what do you need to know about those 8 months, not just today?
objectives: Audit historical access, not just current
evidence: departed admin, re-enabled 8 months, key-OU read access

scenarios.title: The Escrow Outage
scenarios.situation: The AD server hosting BitLocker recovery keys goes down during a company-wide Windows update that triggers recovery mode on 300 laptops. Users are locked out; the helpdesk cannot retrieve keys; the outage will last 6 hours.
scenarios.prompt: What does this incident teach about architecture?
choices: Nothing — outages happen, the update was the real problem

Escrow is critical infrastructure: it needs the same HA design as production — replicated stores, tested backups, offline break-glass copies — because recovery demand spikes exactly when systems are stressed
Ban the Windows update that caused it
Tell users to wait 6 hours quietly
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The cruel correlation: the events that trigger mass recovery (bad updates, hardware changes) are the same events that stress infrastructure. A single-server escrow is a single point of failure for the entire fleet's availability. The architecture fix is HA replication, tested restore, and sealed offline break-glass copies for exactly this scenario. Blaming the update (C) misses that updates are inevitable; silence (D) is not a plan.
scenarios.hint: When is recovery demand highest — and what state is your infrastructure in at exactly that moment?
evidence: 300 laptops in recovery, escrow down 6 hours
single AD server, company-wide update trigger

scenarios.title: The VIP Exception
scenarios.situation: The CEO's laptop needs BitLocker recovery while traveling. Policy requires dual approval for executive key retrieval. The CEO's chief of staff demands the key immediately by phone, 'the CEO is waiting,' and hints at escalation.
choices: Release the key — the CEO outranks the policy
Refuse outright — policy is policy, no exceptions

Follow the policy's emergency path: verify the requester's identity strongly, get the second approver on the line (expedited, not skipped), retrieve with full logging — the policy should define fast, not absent, for VIPs
Have the chief of staff approve it themselves as the second approver
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. VIP pressure is the classic social-engineering vector — 'the CEO is waiting' is also exactly what an attacker says. But rigid refusal (B) teaches executives that security is the enemy, breeding future circumvention. The mature design has an expedited-but-complete emergency path: strong verification, real second approval (fast, via phone), full logging. Caving (A) or self-approval (D) voids the control that protects the CEO's own data.
scenarios.hint: Is this urgency real — and would a real attacker sound any different?
objectives: Verify VIP requests, don't waive them
Treat urgency as a verification trigger
evidence: CEO key retrieval, phone demand, escalation hint
dual approval required for executive keys

scenarios.title: The Migration Gap
scenarios.situation: You are migrating escrow from on-prem AD to a cloud vault. The plan: bulk-export all keys, import to the new vault, then decommission AD. During the 3-week migration window, both systems hold all keys.
scenarios.prompt: What is the biggest risk, and the fix?
choices: User confusion during the window — send more communications
The cloud vault's uptime SLA — negotiate harder
Nothing — migrations are routine

The export file — a bulk plaintext export of every recovery key is the crown jewels in transit; encrypt it, minimize its lifetime, verify import completeness, then securely destroy the export and the old store
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. A bulk export concentrates every key the enterprise owns into one file — the highest-value target the company will ever create. Its lifetime must be measured in hours, encrypted at rest and in transit, handled by named custodians, with verified import (key counts reconciled) before destruction of both the export and the decommissioned store. Communications (A) and SLAs (B) matter, but neither addresses a plaintext copy of all keys.
scenarios.hint: For a few hours, where does every key in the company live — and who could reach it?
objectives: Treat migration as the highest-risk window
evidence: bulk export of all recovery keys

scenarios.title: The Coverage Gap
scenarios.situation: Your quarterly escrow audit: 11,200 encrypted laptops in inventory, 10,640 keys in escrow — 95% coverage. The missing 560 are mostly remote workers whose devices 'failed to escrow at provisioning and nobody followed up.'
choices: Launch a targeted remediation: identify the 560, push escrow enrollment via policy/MDM with a deadline, track to 99%+, and fix the provisioning check so failures alert instead of silently passing
Re-image all 560 devices to force re-enrollment
Blame the remote workers for not following instructions
Accept 95% — that is a good score
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Five percent of an 11,200-device fleet is 560 unrecoverable disks — 560 potential data-loss incidents and 560 audit findings wearing a trench coat. Coverage is binary per device: a missing key is a missing control. Targeted re-enrollment plus a provisioning gate (fail-closed: no escrow, no compliance) fixes both the backlog and the leak. Re-imaging (B) is a sledgehammer; acceptance (D) normalizes the gap.
scenarios.hint: Is 95% a good score — or 560 missing controls?
objectives: Treat coverage as binary per device

scenarios.title: The Departing Key Custodian
scenarios.situation: Your senior PKI/escrow administrator — one of two people with vault master access — resigns with two weeks' notice. They are professional and cooperative, but they know every escrow architecture detail and hold break-glass credentials.
choices: Throw a farewell lunch — they are cooperative, no risk

Execute the privileged-departure playbook: rotate vault master credentials and break-glass secrets on their last day, review their recent access logs for anomalies, transfer custodianship formally to a named successor, and update the access roster — trust the person, verify the transition
Revoke everything today and walk them out — zero trust means zero notice
Do nothing until the exit interview
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Privileged departures get a playbook, not a personality assessment: cooperative or not, standing credentials must rotate because you cannot un-know a secret, access logs get a final review, and custodianship transfers formally. The farewell lunch (A) confuses likability with risk management; immediate walkout (C) burns bridges and may violate employment terms; waiting (D) leaves the window open. Professional departures still get the full protocol — that is what makes it professional.
scenarios.hint: What secrets does this person know that you cannot un-tell them — and what rotates because of that?
evidence: senior escrow admin, 2 weeks notice, cooperative

domains.summary: Managing recovery keys at fleet scale.

domains.name: Cloud Encryption

scenarios.title: Whose Key Is It?
scenarios.situation: Your team stores customer PII in cloud object storage with provider-managed default encryption. A customer contract now requires customer-managed keys with annual rotation and audit logs of key usage. Legal asks if you are compliant today.
scenarios.prompt: What is the honest answer and the fix?
choices: Yes — the data is encrypted with AES-256, which satisfies the requirement
No — provider-managed keys fail the contract's control requirements; migrate the buckets to customer-managed keys (CMK), enable rotation and key-use logging, and document the mapping
Mostly — add a note to the contract that provider encryption is equivalent
Encrypt the data a second time client-side and keep provider encryption too
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Provider-managed encryption protects against infrastructure threats but gives you no key control, no rotation, and no usage audit — the contract requires all three. 'AES-256' (A) answers the algorithm question nobody asked; contract notes (C) do not create controls; double encryption (D) adds complexity without key governance. Migrate to CMK with rotation and logging, then evidence it.
scenarios.hint: Who controls the key today — you, or the provider? What does the contract require?
evidence: customer-managed keys, annual rotation, usage audit logs

scenarios.title: The KMS Outage
scenarios.situation: Your application decrypts data keys via KMS on every request. The KMS region has an outage. Your app is down — not degraded, down — because every request needs a fresh Decrypt call.
scenarios.prompt: What architecture change fixes this class of failure?
choices: Cache decrypted data keys in memory with a TTL (e.g., 10 minutes): KMS calls drop 99%+, the app survives KMS blips, and key rotation still propagates within the TTL window
Remove encryption — availability beats confidentiality
Retry KMS calls with exponential backoff until it recovers
Multi-region KMS keys with failover — same pattern, more regions
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Data-key caching is the standard pattern: the KEK stays in KMS, data keys live briefly in memory, and rotation propagates at TTL expiry — availability and security composed instead of traded. Multi-region (D) helps regional outages but keeps the per-request dependency; retries (C) just wait loudly; dropping encryption (B) surrenders the control. Design for the KMS being unreachable — it will be, eventually.
scenarios.hint: Does every request truly need a live KMS call — or can the data key safely live for minutes?
objectives: Cache data keys, not master keys
evidence: KMS region down → app fully down

scenarios.title: The Snapshot Leak
scenarios.situation: An engineer shares a database snapshot with a partner's cloud account for debugging. The database is encrypted with your CMK. The partner reports they cannot read it — and asks you to 'just re-share it unencrypted for now.'
choices: Send them a SQL dump over email instead — faster
Refuse all sharing — data never leaves the account
Re-share unencrypted — debugging is urgent and the partner is trusted
Share the snapshot with explicit CMK key-grant to the partner's account, scoped and time-bound, with the sharing logged — the encryption boundary extends deliberately, not accidentally
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Cross-account sharing with explicit key grants extends the encryption boundary under control: scoped to the snapshot, time-bound, logged, revocable. Unencrypted re-sharing (C) or email dumps (A) abandon the boundary for convenience; blanket refusal (B) blocks legitimate work and teaches teams to circumvent you. The CMK grant mechanism exists precisely for this — use the designed path.
scenarios.hint: How do you extend the encryption boundary without breaking it?

scenarios.title: The Logging Gap
scenarios.situation: A compliance audit asks: 'Show us every use of the payments CMK in the last 90 days.' Your KMS has no centralized log export; the console shows recent events only.
choices: Say the logs aged out per retention policy
Export what the console shows and explain the rest verbally
Enable KMS/CloudTrail audit logging to immutable centralized storage immediately, backfill what history exists, document the gap period honestly, and set alerts on anomalous key use going forward
Rotate the key — a fresh key has a clean history
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Key-use auditability is a control, not a convenience: enable centralized immutable logging now, honestly document the blind period (auditors respect disclosed gaps; they punish discovered ones), and alert on anomalies going forward. Console screenshots (B) are not evidence; rotation (D) does not create history; claiming retention policy (A) for logs you never configured is misrepresentation.
scenarios.hint: Can you prove who used the key and when — and if not, what do you tell the auditor?
objectives: Log key use centrally and immutably

scenarios.title: The Departed Key Admin
scenarios.situation: Your sole KMS key administrator leaves abruptly. They created all CMKs, hold the break-glass credentials, and documented nothing. The keys work — for now.
choices: Immediately: rotate break-glass credentials, audit key policies for backdoor access, establish dual-control administration with a named successor, and document the hierarchy — standing admin access in unknown hands is the emergency
Do nothing — the keys work and the admin left professionally
Delete all CMKs and start over
Hire a replacement first — then deal with the keys
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. A departed sole key admin is a standing-privilege emergency regardless of how professional the departure was: rotate the break-glass secrets, audit policies for hidden grants, and end single-person key control with dual administration. Hiring first (D) leaves the window open for months; doing nothing (B) confuses a working system with a secure one; mass deletion (C) destroys production data access.
scenarios.hint: What can that former admin still do today — and what ends that ability?
objectives: Audit key policies for hidden grants
evidence: sole key admin departed, undocumented, break-glass held

scenarios.title: The Multi-Cloud Key Mess
scenarios.situation: After acquisitions, you have AWS KMS keys, Azure Key Vault keys, and GCP KMS keys — three consoles, three IAM models, no inventory. Leadership asks: 'Are we compliant?'
choices: Consolidate everything into one cloud's KMS immediately
Build the inventory first: every key, its owner, rotation status, and what data it protects — across all three clouds — then rationalize; you cannot govern what you cannot list
Declare compliance — all three providers are reputable
Hire a consultant to answer the question
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Governance starts with inventory: an authoritative list of keys, owners, rotation state, and data classification across providers. Consolidation (A) before inventory risks breaking unknown dependencies; declaring compliance (C) is fiction; consultants (D) will ask for the inventory first anyway. The inventory usually reveals the quick wins — orphaned keys, flat keying, missing rotation — that become the rationalization plan.
scenarios.hint: How many keys do you have, and what does each one protect — can you answer that today?
objectives: Turn inventory into a remediation plan

scenarios.title: The Plaintext Hop
scenarios.situation: Your architecture review finds service-to-service traffic inside the VPC uses plaintext HTTP 'because it's internal.' The services handle PII, and VPC flow logs show the traffic crosses availability zones.
choices: Encrypt the payloads but keep HTTP
Accept it — VPCs are private networks
Enforce TLS on every service hop (mTLS ideally), treating the cloud network as untrusted shared infrastructure — 'inside the VPC' is not a security boundary
Move the services into the same availability zone
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Cloud networks are multi-tenant infrastructure operated by the provider — plaintext PII on the wire is exposed to misconfiguration, compromised hosts, and provider-internal access. TLS on every hop (mTLS for service identity) is the standard; same-AZ (D) changes nothing about the trust model; payload-only encryption (A) leaves metadata and is operationally brittle. The data-in-transit state needs its control on every hop.
scenarios.hint: Who else can see traffic 'inside' your VPC — and are you comfortable with all of them reading PII?
evidence: plaintext HTTP service-to-service, PII in transit

scenarios.title: The Rotation That Broke Prod
scenarios.situation: Automated KMS key rotation ran last night. This morning, the application cannot decrypt older database records — the app cached the old data key indefinitely and never re-fetches.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong, and what is the durable fix?
choices: Restore from backup to before the rotation
Re-encrypt the entire database with the new key
Rotation is dangerous — disable automatic rotation

The app violated the envelope contract: data keys must be re-fetched (or cached with TTL) and the sealed data key stored alongside each record must be decrypted with the current KEK version — fix caching to TTL + re-wrap, and keep old KEK versions available during transition
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Rotation is supposed to be safe — the bug is the app's indefinite data-key cache plus missing KEK version handling. The durable fix: TTL-bounded caching, per-record sealed data keys decrypted via the KMS (which handles versioned KEKs), and retaining old KEK versions until re-wrapping completes. Disabling rotation (C) trades a bug for a compliance failure; restore (A) loses a night of data; full re-encryption (B) is the sledgehammer the envelope pattern exists to avoid.
scenarios.hint: Was rotation the problem — or was the app never honoring the envelope contract?
objectives: Honor the envelope contract in code
Fix the bug, keep the rotation
evidence: indefinite data-key cache, no KEK versioning

domains.summary: Encrypting data in AWS/Azure/GCP: KMS, CMKs, and patterns.

domains.name: FDE Incident Response

scenarios.title: The Airport Call
scenarios.situation: A sales director calls from an airport: laptop missing from the security tray 20 minutes ago, contains Q3 forecast data (internal classification). MDM shows the device encrypted, BitLocker healthy, last check-in 25 minutes ago.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct first-hour sequence?
choices: Remote lock + locate attempt, confirm encryption telemetry in the ticket, classify as equipment loss (verified FDE, internal data), notify manager — wipe held in reserve unless the device goes hostile
Do nothing — it will probably turn up at lost and found
Call the airline and wait
Wipe immediately — forecast data is sensitive
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Verified FDE with healthy telemetry makes this equipment loss, not a breach — the proportional response is lock, locate, document, and monitor, with wipe as the escalation if the device shows hostile activity. Immediate wipe (D) destroys recovery odds and forensic options for internal-classification data; doing nothing (B) abandons the response clock; the airline call (C) is fine in parallel but is not the security response.
scenarios.hint: What does the telemetry actually tell you about risk — and what response does that risk level warrant?
objectives: Keep wipe in reserve, not as reflex
evidence: missing 20 min, MDM: encrypted, BitLocker healthy

scenarios.title: The Hostile Logins
scenarios.situation: Two hours after a laptop theft, MDM shows three failed login attempts followed by the device going offline. The laptop holds customer PII (regulated classification). Encryption was verified at last check-in.
choices: Wait for it to come back online — the failed logins show the PIN held

Escalate to breach-class response: execute the pre-defined wipe decision for regulated data, preserve all telemetry as evidence, engage legal for notification analysis — failed logins signal active attack, not loss
Remote-wipe and close the ticket — problem solved
Ask the user to change their password
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Failed logins followed by offline is the hostile pattern: someone is actively working the device, and regulated PII raises the stakes to breach-class. The wipe decision should be pre-defined by data classification (no incident-time debate), telemetry preserved for the investigation, and legal engaged because notification obligations may trigger. Waiting (A) cedes the clock; wipe-and-close (C) skips evidence and legal; password change (D) is a sideshow.
scenarios.hint: Is this still a lost device — or has the pattern changed what you are dealing with?

scenarios.title: The Litigation Surprise
scenarios.situation: A laptop with key project data is stolen. Security prepares the remote wipe — then legal calls: litigation was anticipated last week, the device is under legal hold, and nobody told security.
choices: Wipe it and don't tell legal — what they don't know protects them
Ask the thief to return it
Wipe anyway — the thief has the data, hold is moot

Stand down the wipe immediately: a held device must be preserved — wiping under hold is spoliation. Shift to lock + track + telemetry preservation, and fix the hold-notification process so security learns of holds the same day legal issues them
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Legal hold overrides incident response: wiping a held device is spoliation regardless of the security justification, and sanctions follow the act, not the intent. The secure posture becomes lock, track, and preserve — plus the real fix, a same-day hold-notification channel between legal and security. Wiping anyway (C) or secretly (A) converts an incident into a legal catastrophe.
scenarios.hint: Which risk is larger right now — the thief reading project data, or your company facing spoliation sanctions?
objectives: Honor legal holds over incident reflexes
evidence: litigation anticipated last week, security just learned

scenarios.title: The Unencrypted Exception
scenarios.situation: Post-theft verification finds the stolen laptop was in the 5% exception group: BitLocker deployment 'pending' for 6 weeks due to a TPM driver issue. It held employee HR records. The fleet dashboard showed 95% compliant.
choices: Encrypt HR records separately and move on
Fire the technician who owned the driver issue

Treat exceptions as the actual risk surface: 5% of the fleet is hundreds of unencrypted disks — the dashboard's 95% was comfort, not security. Remediate the exception queue with deadlines and make 'pending' a visible, aging, escalated state
Accept 95% — perfect compliance is impossible
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The exception queue is where incidents live: 'pending' without aging or escalation is a permanent parking lot for risk. Five percent unencrypted in a large fleet is a large absolute number of plaintext disks, and HR records make this a breach with notification duties. The fix is operational: exceptions age visibly, escalate automatically, and get deadlines — plus a post-incident fleet sweep. Blame (B) fixes nothing; acceptance (D) normalizes it.
scenarios.hint: How many unencrypted disks does 95% compliant actually mean — and how long had this one been waiting?
objectives: Manage the exception queue as the risk surface
evidence: BitLocker 'pending' 6 weeks, TPM driver issue, HR records

scenarios.title: The Border Seizure
scenarios.situation: An executive traveling internationally has their laptop seized at a border crossing. They call the security team: officials are demanding the BitLocker PIN. Company policy has no border-search section.
scenarios.prompt: What guidance do you give — and what should have existed?
choices: Give them the PIN — compliance with authorities is mandatory everywhere
Refuse — the data is more important than the executive's travel

Immediate: advise calm compliance with local law while noting what was accessed (laws vary by country; counsel is the authority, not the SOC). Systemic: the travel protocol should have covered this — loaner devices with minimal data for high-risk destinations, pre-travel briefings, and counsel-approved guidance per country
Remote-wipe the device while they hold it
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Border search law varies radically by jurisdiction — the SOC cannot give legal advice in real time, and both blanket compliance (A) and blanket refusal (B) may be wrong depending on the country. The real failure is the missing travel protocol: loaner devices, minimal-data travel images, and pre-trip briefings prevent the dilemma. Wiping during seizure (D) may constitute obstruction. Get counsel involved immediately; build the protocol before the next trip.
scenarios.hint: Should this decision have been made during the seizure — or months before, in a travel protocol?
objectives: Use loaner devices for high-risk destinations
evidence: executive laptop seized at border, PIN demanded

scenarios.title: The Ransomware on Encrypted Disks
scenarios.situation: Ransomware detonates on 40 endpoints — all BitLocker-encrypted. The ransomware encrypted user files on top of the FDE. An executive asks: 'But the disks were encrypted — how did this happen?'
scenarios.prompt: What is the accurate explanation and the response priority?
choices: Decrypt the disks to remove the ransomware faster
Pay the ransom — the encryption layers make recovery impossible
FDE failed — re-evaluate the encryption vendor

FDE worked as designed: it protects powered-off disks from theft, not running systems from malware — the ransomware ran as the authenticated user, whom FDE transparently serves. Priority: incident response (isolate, restore from encrypted backups), then the honest stakeholder education
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. This is the unlocked-machine principle at fleet scale: FDE decrypts for authorized running processes, and ransomware is (from the disk's perspective) an authorized process. No vendor failed; the threat model was misunderstood. The response is standard IR — isolate, assess, restore from clean encrypted backups — plus the stakeholder correction, because the executive's mental model ('encrypted = safe from everything') will misdirect the next budget discussion.
scenarios.hint: Who did FDE think the ransomware was — and why did it serve the files?
evidence: ransomware on 40 BitLocker endpoints, files encrypted over FDE

scenarios.title: The Wipe Confirmation
scenarios.situation: You remote-wiped a stolen laptop holding regulated data. MDM reports 'wipe command sent.' Legal asks: 'Can you confirm the data is destroyed?'
scenarios.prompt: What is the honest, complete answer?
choices: 'Wipe command sent and acknowledged by the device at [timestamp]; last telemetry [time]. Full destruction cannot be confirmed for a device outside our custody — the MDM acknowledgment is our evidence, and here is what it does and does not prove.' Then document the evidence chain for the breach file
No — assume the data is compromised and notify everyone
Wait a week and check again
Yes — the command was sent, the data is destroyed
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. 'Command sent' is not 'data destroyed' — honesty about the evidence gap is both legally safer and professionally correct. The acknowledgment timestamp plus telemetry is real evidence; claiming certainty you do not have (D) creates liability when challenged; assuming compromise (B) may trigger unnecessary notifications; waiting (C) is not a verification strategy. Document what the evidence proves and its limits — that is the breach file's job.
scenarios.hint: What does 'wipe command sent' actually prove — and what would prove destruction?
objectives: Give legal precise, not comforting, answers

scenarios.title: The Reappearing Device
scenarios.situation: A laptop reported stolen 3 weeks ago — wiped, ticket closed — suddenly checks into MDM from a new location, healthy, encrypted, with the wipe apparently never executing (it was offline). It holds no regulated data.
choices: Ignore it — the ticket is closed

Treat it as a new incident: quarantine the device in MDM, verify encryption and escrow state, investigate the 3-week gap (what ran on it, what data was accessed), then decide: re-wipe, reimage, or return to service — closed tickets reopen when devices do
Wipe it again immediately without investigation
Return it to the user — it's healthy
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. A reappearing device is a new incident with a 3-week unknown: quarantine first (network containment), verify state, investigate the gap, then decide disposition. Ignoring (A) leaves a potentially-compromised device on the network; blind re-wipe (C) destroys the forensic value of the gap; returning it (D) trusts 3 weeks of unknown custody. The wipe that never executed is also a process finding — offline-device wipe reliability goes in the playbook review.
scenarios.hint: What happened during the 3 weeks you weren't watching — and how would you know?
objectives: Reopen closed tickets for reappearing devices
evidence: stolen 3 wks ago, wiped (never executed — offline), now checking in

lessons.title: Full-Disk Encryption & Endpoint Hardening — Core concepts
concepts: Full-disk encryption protects data at rest: when the machine is off, the disk is ciphertext without the key. It does nothing for a running, unlocked system — that is the endpoint hardening layer's job.

BitLocker protectors define pre-boot authentication: TPM-only is transparent (weakest), TPM + PIN adds something you know, and a startup key adds something you have. Match the protector to the data's value.
LUKS gives Linux the same guarantee with up to eight key slots per volume: one passphrase per person, clean revocation on departure, and header backups stored separately from the disk.
Keys need a lifecycle: generate securely, escrow recovery keys in a separate audited system (never on the volume they unlock), restrict and log access, and rotate or revoke on personnel changes.
Endpoint hardening completes the picture: Secure Boot, Kernel DMA Protection, short screen-lock timeouts, and managed removable media cover the attacks that encryption alone cannot.

example.code: manage-bde -status C:
example.walkthrough: On Windows, this reports BitLocker's state for the drive: encryption method, protectors in use, and lock status. Run it during audits to verify policy compliance — 'Protection Status: Protection On' with the expected protector (TPM+PIN, not TPM-only) is what you're checking for.

pitfalls: Common trap: storing the recovery key on the encrypted volume it unlocks — unreachable exactly when needed.
Common trap: believing FDE protects a running unlocked machine — DMA, evil-USB, and unlocked-screen attacks bypass it entirely.
Common trap: sharing one LUKS passphrase across a team — departures become cryptographic emergencies.
Common trap: TPM-only BitLocker on high-value laptops — transparent boot means possession nearly equals access.

Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow
Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

lessons.title: Capstone: Enterprise Encryption Deployment — Blueprint
concepts: Your capstone proves integrated capability: Design and document a complete FDE rollout: technology selection, key management architecture, recovery procedures, and compliance mapping — a deployment plan you'd present to a CISO.
Scope it in milestones, not monoliths. Each milestone is independently demonstrable — if you run out of time, you still have working pieces.
Document as you build. The artifact plus the write-up is what you show; either alone is half the value.
Build in public where appropriate: version control, clear commits, a README that explains the why, not just the what.

CAPSTONE MILESTONES

  2. Design the key management and escrow architecture
  3. Write recovery procedures for all failure modes
  4. Map controls to compliance frameworks
  5. Present the deployment plan as a CISO briefing
example.walkthrough: A capstone is graded on integration and judgment, not just completion. At each milestone ask: 'what decision did I make here, and why this way?'

Building without documenting — you will forget your own reasoning within days.
Perfectionism on milestone 1 — get all milestones to 'working' before polishing any to 'great.'

Screenshots and terminal transcripts beat prose for proving hands-on work. Capture evidence as you go.
Anticipate the three hardest questions about your capstone and write the answers before anyone asks.

Hiding limitations — naming them with a plan reads as maturity.
No reproduction steps — if they can't run it, it doesn't exist.

Connect each capstone decision back to bootcamp domains — this shows integrated understanding, not isolated effort.

Over-running time — a tight 5 minutes beats a rambling 15.
Memorizing a script — know the beats, speak naturally.
