lessons.title: Symmetric Encryption Essentials
concepts: AES is the standard: AES-256-XTS for disk encryption — XTS mode is designed for storage (tweakable, no chaining dependency).
Keys, not algorithms, are the security: AES-256 with a weak password is weaker than AES-128 with a strong one — key management decides.
The key hierarchy: Data Encryption Key (DEK) encrypts data; Key Encryption Key (KEK) wraps the DEK — rotating the KEK doesn't re-encrypt the disk.
Never roll your own crypto: use vetted implementations (BitLocker, LUKS, FileVault) — custom schemes fail in ways experts predict and you won't.

example.code:
KEY HIERARCHY
  DEK (random, per-volume) → encrypts all sectors
  KEK (from password/TPM) → wraps the DEK
  Change password? Re-wrap DEK (seconds).
  Change DEK? Re-encrypt disk (hours).
  Hierarchy makes operations practical.
example.walkthrough: When asked 'how does FDE work,' start with the DEK/KEK hierarchy — it's the architecture everything else hangs on.

pitfalls: Encrypting with the password directly — no KEK layer means password changes re-encrypt everything.
Custom crypto schemes — the graveyard of good intentions.
Ignoring mode: ECB on disks leaks patterns; XTS exists for a reason.
lessons.try_it: Explain why changing a BitLocker PIN takes seconds but changing the DEK takes hours.

lessons.title: Hashing, KDFs, and Authentication
concepts: Passwords become keys via KDFs: PBKDF2, bcrypt, Argon2 — slow, salted, memory-hard functions that make guessing expensive.
Salts defeat rainbow tables: unique salt per volume means precomputed attacks fail — the salt isn't secret, it's unique.
Authenticated encryption (or HMAC) detects tampering: encryption without authentication lets attackers flip bits meaningfully.
Plausible deniability (VeraCrypt hidden volumes): know it exists, know its limits — coerced disclosure defeats most schemes eventually.

example.code:
KDF LADDER
  Raw password → NEVER use directly
  PBKDF2 (100k+ iterations) → baseline
  bcrypt → adaptive cost
  Argon2id → memory-hard, modern best
  Salt: 128-bit random, stored with the volume.
example.walkthrough: The KDF is the bridge between human passwords and cryptographic keys — its strength sets the floor.

pitfalls: Fast hashes (SHA-256) for passwords — GPUs try billions/sec; use KDFs.
No salt — rainbow tables precompute unsalted hashes.
Encryption without authentication — bit-flipping attacks are real.
lessons.try_it: Why is Argon2 preferred over PBKDF2 for new deployments? What attack does memory-hardness defeat?

lessons.title: Threat Model for Disk Encryption
concepts: FDE protects data at rest: stolen/lost devices, improper disposal, seizure — the powered-off attacker is the threat.
FDE does NOT protect running systems: DMA attacks, cold boot, evil maid — powered-on machines need additional controls.
The boundary: FDE's promise ends where the OS boots — everything after is endpoint hardening's job.
Threat-model honestly: FDE + strong pre-boot auth defeats the thief; it doesn't defeat the lab with a logic analyzer.

example.code:
THREAT MATRIX
  Stolen laptop (off) → FDE wins
  Lost USB (off) → FDE wins
  Evil maid (access + time) → FDE + TPM + Secure Boot needed
  Running system seizure → FDE irrelevant; memory forensics apply
  Match controls to the actual adversary.
example.walkthrough: Scope FDE claims precisely — overclaiming ('military-grade unhackable') destroys credibility.

pitfalls: 'Encryption = total security' — the most dangerous sentence in the field.
Ignoring the running-system gap — FDE is one layer, not the stack.
No pre-boot auth — TPM-only without PIN is convenience, not security.
lessons.try_it: Write the threat matrix for your organization: which adversaries does FDE stop?

lessons.title: Compliance Drivers
concepts: Regulations mandate encryption: HIPAA (addressable but expected), PCI-DSS (Req 3), GDPR (Art 32), CMMC (SC.L2-3.13.11) — know your framework's language.
'Addressable' doesn't mean optional: HIPAA addressable requires implementation, documented alternative, or risk acceptance — auditors expect encryption.
Breach safe harbors: encrypted data often exempts from breach notification — the business case in one clause.
Evidence for auditors: deployment reports, key escrow proof, policy documents — compliance is demonstrated, not asserted.

example.code:
COMPLIANCE MAP
  HIPAA §164.312(a)(2)(iv): encryption addressable
  PCI-DSS 3.4/3.5: render PAN unreadable; key management
  GDPR Art 32: 'pseudonymisation and encryption'
  CMMC SC.L2-3.13.11: FIPS-validated cryptography
  Map each control to your implementation.
example.walkthrough: Speak the framework's language to the auditor — control numbers, not vibes.

pitfalls: 'Addressable means optional' — the most expensive misreading in HIPAA.
No evidence package — assertions without artifacts fail audits.
Encryption without key management — the control auditors actually test.
lessons.try_it: Map your FDE deployment to one framework's controls with evidence per control.

lessons.title: BitLocker Architecture
concepts: Protectors: TPM, PIN, USB key, password, recovery key — protectors wrap the volume master key; multiple protectors = multiple unlock paths.
TPM + PIN is the enterprise standard: TPM binds to boot integrity (PCR measurements), PIN adds the human factor — together they defeat evil-maid and theft.
Network Unlock: domain-joined machines unlock automatically on trusted wired networks — convenience without weakening off-network protection.
Used Space Only vs Full: used-space encryption is fast for new deployments; full encryption (including free space) for devices with prior sensitive data.

example.code:
PROTECTOR STACK (enterprise)
  TPM: boot integrity binding (PCRs 0,2,4,11)
  + PIN: 6+ digit pre-boot auth
  + Recovery key: 48-digit escrowed in AD/MBAM
  + Network Unlock: auto-unlock on corp LAN
  Off-network thief: TPM+PIN stops them. IT: recovery key saves users.
example.walkthrough: Design protector stacks by threat: TPM-only is convenience; TPM+PIN is security; escrow is recoverability.

pitfalls: TPM-only on laptops — no pre-boot auth means stolen+PIN-less boots are trivially attacked.
No escrow — one forgotten PIN = one bricked device + data loss.
Used-space-only on used devices — deleted data in 'free' space stays plaintext.
lessons.try_it: Design the protector stack for: executive laptops, lab workstations, kiosk machines.

lessons.title: TPM and Secure Boot Integration
concepts: TPM PCRs measure the boot chain: firmware, bootloader, OS loader — BitLocker seals keys to these measurements; tampering changes PCRs and blocks unlock.
PCR selection matters: binding too many PCRs causes legitimate updates to trigger recovery; too few weakens tamper detection — 0,2,4,11 is the common balance.
Secure Boot + BitLocker: Secure Boot verifies bootloaders cryptographically; BitLocker verifies measurements — layered, complementary.
TPM ownership and clearing: clearing the TPM (e.g., motherboard replacement) destroys sealed keys — recovery key or re-provisioning required.

example.code:
BOOT CHAIN OF TRUST
  UEFI Secure Boot → verifies bootloader signature
  Bootloader → measured into PCRs
  BitLocker → unseals only if PCRs match
  OS → runs on verified chain
  Break any link → no unlock. That's the point.
example.walkthrough: When BitLocker drops to recovery after updates, suspect PCR drift — that's the mechanism working as designed.

pitfalls: Over-binding PCRs — every firmware update becomes a recovery event.
Clearing TPM without escrow — keys destroyed, data inaccessible.
Disabling Secure Boot 'to fix' recovery — destroys the chain's value.
lessons.try_it: A fleet hits recovery after a firmware update. Diagnose using PCR logic and write the remediation.

lessons.title: BitLocker Deployment at Scale
concepts: Group Policy/MDM: enforce encryption, protector requirements, and escrow centrally — unmanaged BitLocker is shadow IT.
MBAM or native AD escrow: recovery keys MUST escrow to AD (or MBAM/MEM) — the recovery password is useless if it's on the encrypted drive.
Compliance reporting: query escrow status and encryption state across the fleet — 'percent encrypted with escrowed keys' is the CISO metric.
Staged rollout: pilot → IT → executives → general — each stage validates policy before the next scale-up.

example.code:
ROLLOUT PLAN
  Week 1-2: Pilot (IT, 50 devices), validate GPO + escrow
  Week 3-4: Executives + high-risk (100)
  Week 5-8: General fleet, phased by department
  Throughout: escrow verification reports, helpdesk recovery drills
  Measure: % encrypted, % escrowed, recovery MTTR.
example.walkthrough: Escrow verification is the rollout's heartbeat — unescrowed encryption is a data-loss program.

pitfalls: No escrow enforcement — the #1 BitLocker deployment failure.
Big-bang rollout — policy bugs at scale are unrecoverable at scale.
No helpdesk recovery drills — first recovery during a real crisis.
lessons.try_it: Write the GPO settings for: require TPM+PIN, enforce escrow, minimum PIN length 6.

lessons.title: BitLocker Recovery Operations
concepts: Recovery triggers: PCR mismatch, PIN failures, hardware changes, malicious tampering — recovery is the safety net, not a failure.
The 48-digit recovery key: each 6-digit group has a checksum digit — typos are caught per-group; read it carefully, group by group.
Helpdesk flow: verify user identity, retrieve escrowed key, read it back twice, document the incident — recovery is a security event.
Post-recovery: investigate the trigger (was it an update? tampering?), re-seal or re-provision as appropriate — don't just unlock and forget.

example.code:
RECOVERY RUNBOOK
  1. Verify user identity (per policy)
  2. Retrieve key from AD/MBAM escrow
  3. Read 48 digits in 8 groups; user confirms each
  4. Unlock; investigate trigger
  5. Re-seal (suspend/resume) or re-provision
  6. Log the incident
  Recovery without investigation is negligence.
example.walkthrough: Drill recovery before you need it — the first real recovery shouldn't be anyone's first.

pitfalls: Reading the key wrong — group-by-group readback prevents typos.
Skipping identity verification — social engineers love 'BitLocker recovery.'
No post-recovery investigation — tampering looks like glitches until examined.
lessons.try_it: Run a tabletop: user calls from an airport, BitLocker recovery screen. Walk the runbook.

lessons.title: LUKS Architecture
concepts: LUKS header: stores key slots, salts, and parameters in a standardized on-disk format — the header IS the key management.
8 key slots: multiple passphrases/keys unlock the same volume — each slot independently revocable; slot 0 isn't special after setup.
Anti-forensic splitter: key material is spread across the disk so no single sector reveals it — wiping the header destroys access.
LUKS2 improvements: Argon2 KDF, authenticated encryption, flexible metadata — prefer LUKS2 for new deployments.

example.code:
LUKS LAYOUT
  [PHDR: magic, version, cipher, slots]
  [Key slot 0: salt, iterations, key material]
  [Key slot 1: ...]
  [Encrypted data...]
  Header backup (luksHeaderBackup) is mandatory — header loss = data loss.
example.walkthrough: Back up LUKS headers before any operation — the header is a single point of failure for the entire volume.

pitfalls: No header backup — one corrupted sector bricks terabytes.
LUKS1 by default on old tools — specify --type luks2.
Forgetting slot management — ex-employees' slots stay valid until revoked.
lessons.try_it: Create a LUKS2 volume, add a second key slot, back up the header, then revoke the first slot.

lessons.title: Linux FDE Deployment
concepts: Distribution installers (Ubuntu, RHEL) offer FDE via LUKS+LVM — the standard path; manual setup is for special cases.
LVM on LUKS: encrypt the physical volume, then layer LVM inside — one passphrase unlocks all logical volumes.
/boot stays unencrypted (or with Grub + LUKS for /boot) — the initramfs unlocks the root volume; Secure Boot attests the boot chain.
Remote unlock: Dropbear SSH in initramfs for headless servers — unlock via SSH without physical console access.

example.code:
SERVER FDE STACK
  /boot: unencrypted (or LUKS w/ Grub)
  initramfs: prompts (or Dropbear SSH) for passphrase
  LUKS2 → LVM → root/swap/home
  TPM2 + Clevis: auto-unlock on trusted boot (servers)
  Headless? Dropbear. Datacenter? TPM2+NetworkBoundDisk.
example.walkthrough: Match the unlock method to the server's reality: console access, network trust, and threat model.

pitfalls: No remote unlock on headless servers — every reboot needs a datacenter trip.
Unencrypted swap — swap contains memory contents; encrypt it too.
Single passphrase, no escrow — the Linux equivalent of no BitLocker escrow.
lessons.try_it: Design FDE for: a headless colo server, a developer laptop, an edge device. Compare.

lessons.title: Key Management for LUKS
concepts: Passphrase quality: the KDF can't save 'password123' — enforce strong passphrases; consider FIDO2/token-based unlock.
Key files: high-entropy files as key slots for servers (TPM-sealed or USB-stored) — better than typed passphrases for machines.
Escrow: store header backups + slot passphrases in the enterprise vault — LUKS has no AD equivalent; build the process.
Rotation: add new slot, verify, revoke old — rotation without re-encryption, thanks to the key-slot design.

example.code:
KEY LIFECYCLE
  Provision: strong passphrase + escrowed backup
  Operate: unlock via primary slot
  Rotate: add slot N+1 → verify → revoke slot N
  Decommission: revoke all slots + cryptsetup erase
  Slots make rotation cheap — use them.
example.walkthrough: Document the slot inventory per volume: which slot, whose credential, when rotated.

pitfalls: One slot forever — no rotation, no revocation path.
Passphrase in a ticket/email — the escrow must be a vault, not chat.
No decommission procedure — retired disks with valid slots are breaches.
lessons.try_it: Rotate a LUKS key slot: add, verify, revoke. Document each step.

lessons.title: Forensics and Data Recovery
concepts: Header backup = recovery: with the header backup and any valid slot credential, data recovers to any Linux system.
Damaged headers: photorec-style carving fails on encrypted data — header integrity is everything; keep multiple backups.
Secure erase: cryptsetup erase wipes key slots — data becomes cryptographically unrecoverable without re-encrypting terabytes.
Legal considerations: key disclosure laws vary by jurisdiction — know the legal framework before promising 'unbreakable.'

example.code:
RECOVERY MATRIX
  Header OK + key OK → full recovery
  Header OK + key lost → brute force (usually infeasible)
  Header damaged + backup → restore backup, recover
  Header damaged, no backup → data lost (cryptographically)
  The backup is the entire DR plan.
example.walkthrough: Test header restore annually — untested backups are rumors.

pitfalls: No tested header restores — the DR plan is theoretical.
Keys and headers stored together — one incident takes both.
Promising legal immunity — disclosure laws exist; counsel decides.
lessons.try_it: Simulate: back up a header, damage the original, restore, verify data.

lessons.title: TPM Capabilities
concepts: The TPM is a crypto coprocessor: sealed storage, attestation, RNG — hardware-backed keys that never leave the chip.
Sealing binds data to PCR state: unseal only succeeds if boot measurements match — tampering breaks the seal.
TPM 2.0 vs 1.2: 2.0 is the current standard (algorithm agility, more banks); 1.2 is legacy — know which you're deploying.
Ownership: taking TPM ownership establishes the hierarchy; clearing destroys sealed data — plan ownership lifecycle.

example.code:
TPM PRIMITIVES
  Seal: encrypt to PCR state
  Unseal: decrypt iff PCRs match
  Quote: sign PCRs for remote attestation
  RNG: hardware entropy source
  Four primitives; everything builds on them.
example.walkthrough: Design with TPM primitives, not TPM magic — each has specific guarantees and limits.

pitfalls: 'TPM = secure' without PCR design — unconfigured sealing proves nothing.
Clearing without escrow — sealed data dies with the clear.
TPM 1.2 on new deployments — legacy crypto, limited future.
lessons.try_it: List the four TPM primitives and one use case each.

lessons.title: Secure Boot Chains
concepts: Secure Boot verifies each boot stage cryptographically: UEFI → bootloader → kernel — unsigned code doesn't run.
The chain of trust: each stage verifies the next before executing — break one link, boot stops.
Keys: PK (platform), KEK (key exchange), db (allowed), dbx (forbidden) — key management is the operational reality.
Linux and Secure Boot: shim bootloaders carry Microsoft signatures; custom kernels need MOK enrollment.

example.code:
BOOT CHAIN
  UEFI (PK/KEK/db) → verifies shim
  Shim → verifies GRUB
  GRUB → verifies kernel
  Kernel → verifies modules
  Each link signed; each verified before execution.
example.walkthrough: Secure Boot's value is proportional to key hygiene — sloppy keys, theater security.

pitfalls: Disabling to 'fix' boot issues — destroys the chain's value.
Ignoring MOK management — custom kernels need enrollment.
No dbx updates — revoked bootloaders stay trusted.
lessons.try_it: Explain what happens at each chain link if verification fails.

lessons.title: Measured Boot and Attestation
concepts: Measured boot: each component hashes the next into PCRs — the TPM records what booted, creating an audit trail.
Remote attestation: the TPM quotes PCRs to a verifier — 'prove you're running approved software' without trusting the reporter.
Sealed-vs-attested: sealing protects local data; attestation proves state remotely — different primitives, different problems.
Enterprise use: attestation gates network access (NAC) and key release — unhealthy machines get quarantined automatically.

example.code:
ATTESTATION FLOW
  Verifier → nonce to client
  TPM quotes PCRs + nonce → signed blob
  Verifier checks signature + PCR values vs policy
  Match → access granted; mismatch → quarantine
  Trust the TPM, not the OS's self-report.
example.walkthrough: Attestation moves trust from 'the machine says so' to 'the hardware proves so.'

pitfalls: Confusing measured with secure boot — measuring records; secure boot enforces.
No verifier infrastructure — attestation needs the checking side built.
Ignoring nonce freshness — replayed quotes lie.
lessons.try_it: Design an attestation-gated VPN: what gets measured, who verifies, what happens on mismatch?

lessons.title: TPM Provisioning Lifecycle
concepts: Provisioning: take ownership, configure PCR banks, establish endorsement hierarchy — planned, scripted, verified.
Deprovisioning: clear on retirement/reassignment — sealed data must be unrecoverable before the machine changes hands.
Firmware updates: TPM firmware itself needs updating (vulnerabilities exist) — plan the update with key backup.
Inventory: track TPM versions fleet-wide — 1.2 stragglers are the technical debt to retire.

example.code:
TPM LIFECYCLE
  Procure: verify 2.0, firmware current
  Provision: ownership + PCR config (scripted)
  Operate: monitor, update firmware as needed
  Retire: clear + verify + document
  Lifecycle, not one-time setup.
example.walkthrough: TPM at fleet scale is lifecycle management — provisioning is day one of years.

pitfalls: No deprovisioning — retired machines carry sealed secrets.
Untracked versions — 1.2 machines hide in the fleet.
Manual provisioning — script it or it drifts.
lessons.try_it: Write the TPM provisioning runbook: 10 steps from unboxing to verified.

lessons.title: Escrow Architecture
concepts: Escrow is mandatory: every encryption deployment needs key recovery — the business can't accept unrecoverable data.
Segregation: escrow databases need their own access controls, auditing, and encryption — the keys to the kingdom need a kingdom-grade vault.
AD/MBAM for BitLocker, vaults for LUKS, MDM for mobile — use the platform's native escrow, but verify it actually works.
Access procedure: who can retrieve, under what authorization, with what logging — the policy is as important as the technology.

example.code:
ESCROW STACK
  Storage: dedicated vault/HSM-backed DB
  Access: break-glass + ticketed retrieval
  Audit: every access logged, reviewed
  Test: quarterly retrieval drills
  Escrow you can't retrieve under pressure isn't escrow.
example.walkthrough: Test retrieval quarterly — untested escrow is theoretical escrow.

pitfalls: No escrow — the #1 encryption deployment failure.
Escrow without access controls — the vault becomes the target.
Untested retrieval — discover the failure during the crisis.
lessons.try_it: Document your escrow architecture: storage, access, audit, testing.

lessons.title: Rotation Policies
concepts: Rotate on events: personnel departure, suspected compromise, scheduled intervals — event-driven beats calendar-only.
BitLocker rotation: change PINs/passwords freely (KEK re-wrap, seconds); DEK rotation needs re-encryption (hours) — know the difference.
LUKS rotation: add-verify-revoke slots — no re-encryption needed; the slot design makes rotation cheap.
Document every rotation: what changed, when, why, verified by whom — the audit trail is the compliance artifact.

example.code:
ROTATION MATRIX
  BitLocker PIN → re-wrap (seconds)
  BitLocker DEK → re-encrypt (hours)
  LUKS slot → add/verify/revoke (minutes)
  FileVault → institutional key rotation
  Know your operation's cost before promising its frequency.
example.walkthrough: Match rotation frequency to operation cost — expensive rotations happen rarely; cheap ones happen often.

pitfalls: Promising DEK rotation quarterly — the re-encryption cost is prohibitive.
No rotation ever — static credentials decay.
Unlogged rotations — unauditable security is unprovable security.
lessons.try_it: Write rotation procedures for each platform you manage, with costs.

lessons.title: HSMs and Key Vaults
concepts: HSMs: tamper-resistant hardware for key operations — keys never leave the module; operations happen inside.
Cloud KMS (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault): HSM-backed key management as a service — the pragmatic enterprise choice.
Bring-your-own-key (BYOK): customer HSMs backing cloud KMS — control with cloud convenience; know the trade-offs.
Cost reality: HSMs are expensive and operationally heavy — use them where the key's value justifies it.

example.code:
KEY TIERS
  Tier 1 (HSM): CA keys, master escrow keys
  Tier 2 (Cloud KMS): application keys, data keys
  Tier 3 (Software vault): operational secrets
  Tier by value; spend protection proportionally.
example.walkthrough: Not every key needs an HSM — tier protection to key value.

pitfalls: HSM for everything — cost and complexity without proportional benefit.
Software vault for master keys — the crown jewels need hardware.
No tiering — flat protection wastes money and attention.
lessons.try_it: Tier your organization's keys into three levels with protection per tier.

lessons.title: Lifecycle and Destruction
concepts: Key lifecycle: generate → distribute → use → rotate → retire → destroy — each phase needs procedures.
Destruction standards: NIST 800-88 (Clear/Purge/Destroy) — match the method to the data's classification.
Crypto-shredding: destroying keys renders ciphertext unrecoverable — the fastest sanitization for encrypted media.
Witness and document: destruction needs two-person integrity and certificates — the audit trail outlives the keys.

example.code:
DESTRUCTION DECISION
  Low sensitivity → Clear (overwrite)
  High sensitivity → Purge (firmware commands)
  Top secret → Destroy (physical)
  Encrypted media → Crypto-shred (kill keys)
  Match method to classification; document everything.
example.walkthrough: Destruction is a security control — treat it with control discipline.

pitfalls: Informal disposal — 'throw it away' isn't a sanitization method.
No witnesses — single-person destruction is unauditable.
Keeping retired keys 'just in case' — retired means destroyed.
lessons.try_it: Write the media sanitization procedure for each classification level.

lessons.title: Mobile Platform Encryption
concepts: iOS: Data Protection with Secure Enclave — file-level keys, hardware-bound, wiped on excessive passcode failures.
Android: file-based encryption (FBE) with TrustZone/StrongBox — Direct Boot allows alarms before first unlock.
MDM enforcement: require encryption, set passcode policies, enable remote wipe — unmanaged mobile is unencrypted mobile.
The first-unlock boundary: mobile crypto is strongest before first unlock (BFU); after (AFU), keys linger in memory — know the distinction.

example.code:
MOBILE STATES
  BFU (before first unlock): strongest — keys evicted
  AFU (after first unlock): functional, keys in memory
  MDM: enforce encryption + wipe capability
  Lost phone in BFU + strong passcode = well protected.
example.walkthrough: BFU vs AFU is the mobile threat-model core — seizure state determines resistance.

pitfalls: Assuming locked = encrypted-equivalent — AFU has a larger attack surface.
No MDM on BYOD with corporate data — unmanaged = unprotected.
Weak passcodes — 4-digit PINs fall to brute force; enforce length.
lessons.try_it: Compare BFU and AFU protections for iOS. When does each apply?

lessons.title: Removable Media Policy
concepts: USB drives: the exfiltration vector — policy options range from encrypted-only to blocked, by data classification.
Hardware-encrypted USB: PIN-pad drives (iStorage, Kingston) — encryption without host software, platform-independent.
Software options: BitLocker To Go, LUKS, VeraCrypt — centrally manageable where the platform allows.
DLP integration: endpoint agents can enforce 'encrypted USB or no USB' — technical enforcement beats policy documents.

example.code:
USB DECISION TREE
  Data classification high? → block or hardware-encrypted only
  Medium? → BitLocker To Go enforced via policy
  Low? → allow, audit
  Unknown device? → default deny
  Classify first, then enforce technically.
example.walkthrough: Policy without technical enforcement is a suggestion — DLP agents make it real.

pitfalls: Paper policy, open USB ports — unenforced policy is theater.
No classification — one rule for all data misfires both ways.
Ignoring personal USB — BYOD media is the gap.
lessons.try_it: Draft the USB policy for three data classifications with enforcement per tier.

lessons.title: Secure Disposal of Mobile
concepts: Crypto-erase for mobile: factory reset + key destruction — modern phones make this fast and effective.
MDM remote wipe: the lost-device response — but verify wipe acknowledgment; offline devices can't comply.
The resale trap: 'deleted' photos recoverable without crypto-erase — proper wipe is cryptographic, not just deletion.
Certificate and VPN profile cleanup: deprovisioned devices must lose corporate credentials, not just data.

example.code:
DISPOSAL CHECKLIST
  ☐ Remote wipe issued + acknowledged
  ☐ Crypto-erase verified (factory reset)
  ☐ MDM unenrolled, profiles removed
  ☐ Certificates revoked
  ☐ Asset record updated
  Data + credentials + records — all three.
example.walkthrough: Disposal isn't deletion — it's the verified end of the data lifecycle.

pitfalls: Simple delete and resell — recoverable data, breach waiting.
No wipe acknowledgment — offline devices keep the data.
Forgotten certificates — credentials outlive the device.
lessons.try_it: Write the mobile disposal runbook: 8 steps with verification per step.

lessons.title: Threats Unique to Mobile
concepts: Smudge and shoulder-surfing: physical observation defeats strong crypto — privacy screens and awareness matter.
Malicious profiles/MDM: rogue configuration profiles intercept traffic — user education on profile installation.
Backup gaps: encrypted device, unencrypted cloud backup — the backup is the weak link; enforce encrypted backups.
Forensic tools (Cellebrite/GrayKey): AFU devices are vulnerable — BFU + strong passcode is the defense; know the limits.

example.code:
MOBILE ATTACK SURFACE
  Physical: smudge, shoulder, seizure (AFU risk)
  Network: rogue profiles, evil WiFi
  Cloud: unencrypted backups
  Supply: malicious chargers (juice jacking)
  Crypto is one layer — the surface is wider.
example.walkthrough: Mobile threat modeling must include the physical and cloud layers — device encryption alone is insufficient.

pitfalls: Encrypted phone, plaintext cloud backup — the backup bypasses the phone.
Ignoring juice jacking — charge-only cables for untrusted ports.
AFU complacency — seizure-state awareness for high-risk users.
lessons.try_it: Threat-model a traveling executive's phone: 6 attack vectors with mitigations.

lessons.title: Data States: At Rest, In Transit, In Use
concepts: Data at rest sits on disks and tapes — this is FDE's home turf. Full-disk encryption guarantees that a powered-off, stolen drive yields nothing but ciphertext.
Data in transit crosses networks — TLS, VPNs, and encrypted protocols own this state. FDE does nothing for packets on the wire; confusing the two is a classic audit finding.
Data in use lives in RAM and CPU registers while the machine runs — the hardest state to protect. Memory forensics, cold-boot attacks, and DMA exploits all target this state.
A complete endpoint strategy covers all three states: FDE for rest, TLS/VPN for transit, and memory protections (IOMMU, secure enclaves, screen lock) for use. One state unguarded is a breach path.

example.code:
THREE STATES — THREE CONTROLS
  AT REST:    FDE (BitLocker/LUKS/FileVault) — protects powered-off media
  IN TRANSIT: TLS 1.2+, VPN, encrypted backups — protects the wire
  IN USE:     IOMMU/VT-d, memory encryption, auto-lock — protects live RAM
  GAP MAP: list each asset, mark which states are covered, close the gaps
example.walkthrough: Build the gap map for three real endpoints you manage. Most shops discover their 'encrypted fleet' has unencrypted backups or unlocked screens — the states they never mapped.

pitfalls: 'We have BitLocker, so we're encrypted' — at rest only; transit and use need their own controls.
Unencrypted backups of encrypted disks — the backup becomes the plaintext copy attackers actually steal.
Ignoring data in use — a logged-in, unlocked laptop is decrypted by design; FDE cannot help you there.
lessons.try_it: Pick one laptop you own. List its three data states and the control covering each. Write down the first gap you find.

lessons.title: What FDE Cannot Do: The Honest Limits
concepts: FDE decrypts data for any running process once you authenticate — malware on a logged-in machine reads files exactly like you do. Encryption is not access control.

The evil-maid attack: an attacker with brief physical access modifies the unencrypted boot loader to capture your passphrase next boot. FDE plus Secure Boot plus TPM sealing is the answer — FDE alone is not.
FDE cannot prove who accessed what: it is a confidentiality control, not an auditing control. Pair it with logging, EDR, and file-access monitoring for the full picture.
Legal compulsion bypasses math: courts can order passphrase disclosure in many jurisdictions, and border agents can demand device access. Know the legal landscape before promising 'unbreakable.'

example.code:
FDE LIMITS CARD (tape to the monitor)
  ✗ Running malware on unlocked machine → FDE transparent, files readable
  ✗ Evil maid (bootloader tamper) → needs Secure Boot + TPM, not just FDE
  ✗ Insider with credentials → encryption obeys authorized users
  ✗ Legal order / border search → math yields to law
  ✓ Stolen powered-off laptop → ciphertext only. This is the promise. Keep it.
example.walkthrough: Print the limits card mentally before every stakeholder conversation. Overselling FDE creates the exact false confidence that causes the incidents it cannot prevent.

pitfalls: Selling FDE as total security — it is one control in a stack, and overselling it kills the budget for the rest.
Forgetting the unlocked state — most endpoint breaches happen on running, authenticated machines.
Promising legal immunity — encryption policy must be written with counsel, not with marketing.
lessons.try_it: Write a two-sentence 'what FDE does and does not do' statement you could give an executive. Test it: does it mention the unlocked machine?

lessons.title: The Human Side: Recovery Keys and Helpdesks
concepts: Every FDE deployment is also a helpdesk deployment: forgotten PINs, changed hardware triggering recovery, and traveling users without network access generate the ticket volume.
The recovery key is the master bypass — whoever holds it can decrypt the disk. Escrow design (who can retrieve, with what approval, logged how) is a security decision, not an IT convenience.
Self-service recovery portals cut ticket volume by 70%+ in mature shops, but only when identity verification is strong: MFA-bound retrieval, manager approval workflows, and full audit trails.
User training is the cheapest FDE control: 'write your recovery key on a sticky note' defeats a $200k deployment. Teach the why (a stolen laptop story) not just the how.

example.code:
RECOVERY OPERATIONS MODEL
  Tier 0 — Self-service: user authenticates with MFA, retrieves own key, logged
  Tier 1 — Helpdesk: verifies identity per script, retrieves with ticket, logged
  Tier 2 — Security approval: executive/VIP or bulk retrieval, dual approval
  NEVER: keys in email, chat, spreadsheets, or sticky notes — escrow system only
example.walkthrough: Map your current recovery path against the three tiers. If tier 0 does not exist, that is your next project — it pays for itself in the first quarter of ticket deflection.

pitfalls: Keys outside escrow — every spreadsheet copy is an uncontrolled master key.
Weak identity proofing at recovery — the helpdesk becomes the attacker's key-retrieval service.
No user training — the most expensive FDE failure is a user who never understood the stakes.
lessons.try_it: Time your current recovery flow end-to-end (real or hypothetical). Write the three steps where an attacker could insert themselves — then design the control for each.

lessons.title: Encryption as a System: Data States and Key Flows
concepts: Encryption is not a product — it is a system of flows: plaintext flows in, keys flow from managers to endpoints, ciphertext flows to storage, and recovery flows run backward when humans forget.
Keys have their own lifecycle inside the system: generated, distributed, used, rotated, revoked, destroyed. A key that cannot be revoked is not a control — it is a hope.
Every flow has a failure mode: key distribution fails (user offline), rotation fails (legacy system pinned), destruction fails (backups keep copies). Design for the failure, not the sunny day.
Map the system before buying the tool: most FDE failures are key-management failures wearing an encryption costume.

example.code:
KEY FLOW MAP
  GENERATE (HSM/KMS) → DISTRIBUTE (escrow, TPM provisioning)
    → USE (unlock at boot, data keys in RAM)
    → ROTATE (schedule + compromise trigger)
    → REVOKE (departed users, lost devices)
    → DESTROY (crypto-shredding, key deletion)
  For each arrow: owner, SLA, failure mode, fallback
example.walkthrough: Draw the key flow map for one real system you touch. The arrow you cannot name an owner for is your next incident — find it on paper before it finds you in production.

pitfalls: Tool-first thinking — buying BitLocker licenses without mapping key flows is buying a lock with no key plan.
Ignoring revocation — the departed admin whose key still works is the breach you scheduled yourself.
No destruction path — keys that cannot die mean data that cannot die; decommissioning becomes theater.
lessons.try_it: Sketch the six-stage key flow for your laptop's encryption. Label the owner of each stage — 'nobody' is an answer that demands action.

lessons.title: Trust Chains: From Silicon to Plaintext
concepts: A trust chain is a sequence of verifications: hardware verifies firmware, firmware verifies bootloader, bootloader verifies OS, OS verifies the user — each link vouching for the next.
Break one link and the chain's promise collapses: a tampered bootloader can capture the FDE passphrase no matter how strong the AES key is. Security is only as strong as the weakest verified link.
TPM measured boot turns the chain into evidence: each stage's hash is recorded in PCRs, so a remote verifier can detect tampering. Sealing FDE keys to PCRs binds decryption to an untampered boot.
Defense in depth means overlapping chains: Secure Boot for integrity, TPM for measurement, FDE for confidentiality, attestation for verification. No single link carries the whole promise.

example.code:
TRUST CHAIN (bottom to top)
  [Silicon: TPM, hardware root of trust]
    → measures → [Firmware/UEFI: Secure Boot verifies signature]
    → measures → [Bootloader: verified, untampered]
    → unlocks → [OS: FDE key released only if PCRs match]
    → authenticates → [User: PIN/biometric/password]
  ATTACK: tamper any layer → PCRs change → key stays sealed → data safe
example.walkthrough: Trace the chain on your own machine: is Secure Boot on? Is the TPM provisioned? Is the FDE key sealed to PCRs? Each 'no' is a link you are trusting without verification.

pitfalls: Assuming the chain — most fleets have Secure Boot off or TPM unprovisioned on a fraction of machines; verify, don't assume.
Single-link reliance — FDE without Secure Boot is a strong lock on a door with no frame.
Forgetting the human link — the chain ends at user authentication; phishing bypasses silicon entirely.
lessons.try_it: Check your machine's three links (Secure Boot status, TPM provisioning, FDE key protectors) and write down the result. Fix the weakest link this week.

lessons.title: Chain of Custody: Evidence You Can Defend
concepts: Chain of custody is the documented history of evidence: who collected it, when, where it was stored, and who touched it. A gap in the chain is a gap the defense will drive through.
Every handoff gets logged: item ID, date/time, releasing party, receiving party, purpose, and condition. If it is not written down, in court it did not happen.
Encryption complicates custody: a powered-on encrypted device must be kept alive (Faraday bag + portable power) or the keys evaporate from RAM — custody now includes power state.
Photograph everything before you touch it: screen state, cables, running processes. The scene as found is evidence; your memory of it is not.

example.code:
CUSTODY LOG (per item)
  Item: [ID]  Collected: [date/time/by]
  Description: [make/model/serial/state: on|off|locked]
  Hash: [SHA-256 of image]  Storage: [location, sealed bag #]
  HANDOFFS: [date] [from] → [to] [reason] [condition]
  POWER: device kept alive? [Y/N] method: [Faraday + battery]
example.walkthrough: Start a custody log template today and use it on your next practice acquisition. The habit of logging before touching is what separates admissible evidence from expensive stories.

pitfalls: Collecting before documenting — the first touch without a photo is the first hole in your chain.
Letting an encrypted device die — power loss on a locked device can mean permanent evidence loss; plan power first.
Verbal handoffs — 'I gave it to Dave' without a log entry is a custody gap.
lessons.try_it: Write a custody log entry for your own phone as if seizing it: describe it, note its power state, and log a hypothetical handoff to a colleague.

lessons.title: Imaging: Bit-for-Bit Capture
concepts: Forensic imaging creates a bit-for-bit copy of storage, including deleted files, slack space, and unallocated areas — everything a logical file copy misses.
Always image through a hardware write-blocker: it physically prevents writes to the source drive, so the original cannot be altered no matter what the software does.
Hash the source and the image (SHA-256) and compare: matching hashes prove the copy is exact. Hash before and after — the two values are your integrity testimony.
Two image formats dominate: raw/dd (universal, simple) and E01 (compressed, with metadata and integrity checks). Choose E01 for casework, raw for maximum tool compatibility.

example.code:
IMAGING WORKFLOW
  1. Document scene + power state (photos first)
  2. Connect source via hardware write-blocker
  3. Hash source → record SHA-256
  4. Acquire image (E01 for casework) → record hash
  5. Verify: source hash == image hash
  6. Work ONLY on the copy — source goes to secure storage
  7. Log every step in the custody record
example.walkthrough: Practice the workflow on a spare USB drive with a write-blocker (even a software one for training). The sequence — hash, image, verify, log — must be muscle memory before a real case.

pitfalls: Working on the original — every analysis step on source media is potential alteration; always work the copy.
Skipping the write-blocker — 'I'll be careful' is not a forensic control.
Hashing only at the end — hash the source first, so later challenges cannot claim you altered it mid-process.
lessons.try_it: Image a spare USB drive following the seven-step workflow. Record both hashes and verify they match — that verification line is your first piece of forensic testimony.

lessons.title: Live vs Dead-Box Forensics
concepts: Dead-box forensics analyzes powered-off media: safe, repeatable, and court-friendly — but encrypted dead disks are bricks without the key, and volatile memory is gone forever.
Live forensics captures a running system: RAM contents, network connections, decrypted volumes, logged-in sessions — the richest evidence, but every capture action alters the system slightly.

The triage decision: if the device is on and encrypted, capturing RAM (for keys) and the decrypted volume state comes before anything else — pulling the plug destroys what FDE was designed to protect against you.
Order of volatility governs live capture: registers/cache → RAM → network state → running processes → disk → logs. Collect the most ephemeral evidence first.

example.code:
LIVE TRIAGE (encrypted device, powered on)
  1. Photograph screen + note logged-in user
  2. Capture RAM immediately (keys live here) — Faraday bag on
  3. Record network connections + running processes
  4. Image logical decrypted volumes while accessible
  5. Document every command run (it alters state — disclose it)
  6. Only then consider transport (keep powered, plan power)
example.walkthrough: Rehearse the triage order until you can recite it: RAM, network, processes, volumes. In a real seizure you get one chance at volatile evidence — order is everything.

pitfalls: Pulling the plug on a live encrypted box — the classic evidence-destroying reflex; FDE thanks you for it.
Undocumented live actions — every command alters state; undisclosed alteration is a cross-examination gift.
Treating live capture as optional — on encrypted devices, volatile evidence is often the only evidence.
lessons.try_it: Write the triage order on an index card from memory, then check it against the lesson. Repeat until the order is automatic.

lessons.title: Encrypted Evidence: Technical and Legal Paths
concepts: Technical path one — live capture: RAM dumps often contain FDE keys, and hibernation/page files may too. Speed matters more than elegance; capture first, analyze later.

Technical path two — escrow and backups: enterprise key escrow, cloud backups, and synced devices frequently hold the key or a plaintext copy. Check the key management system before the cryptanalysis.
Legal path — compelled disclosure: many jurisdictions allow courts to order passphrase disclosure, and border searches have their own rules. Coordinate with counsel; never freelance the law.
Legal path — warrants for providers: cloud backups, escrow services, and device vendors respond to proper legal process. The key you need may sit with a third party, one warrant away.

example.code:
ENCRYPTED EVIDENCE DECISION TREE
  Device ON + encrypted? → RAM capture NOW, then logical imaging
  Device OFF + enterprise? → check escrow (AD/MEM/cloud) for recovery key
  Device OFF + personal? → legal: compelled disclosure / provider warrant
  Cloud-synced? → provider legal process for backups (often plaintext)
  NEVER: brute-force theater on AES-256 — budget reality, not TV
example.walkthrough: Build the decision tree into your seizure checklist. The first question is always power state — it determines whether you are in a minutes-long race or a weeks-long legal process.

pitfalls: Brute-force fantasies — AES-256 does not yield to determination; pursue keys, not ciphertext.
Ignoring escrow — the recovery key in AD is evidence you already own; check there first.
Freelancing legal process — compelled disclosure without counsel's coordination poisons the case.
lessons.try_it: For three hypothetical devices (on/enterprise, off/personal, cloud-synced), write which path of the decision tree you take first and why.

lessons.title: The Forensics Report: Writing for Court
concepts: The report answers four questions: what was examined, what was done, what was found, and what it means — in language a non-technical judge and jury can follow.
Methodology before findings: tools used (with versions), hashes verifying integrity, and every deviation from standard procedure disclosed. Transparency is credibility.
Separate fact from opinion clearly: 'the image hash matched' is fact; 'the timestamps suggest the user was active' is opinion — label it, and stay inside your expertise.
Encryption gets its own section: what was encrypted, what keys were available, what methods accessed the data, and what remains inaccessible. Courts respect honest limits over claimed omniscience.

example.code:
REPORT SKELETON
  1. Engagement & scope (who asked, what devices)
  2. Methodology (tools + versions, hashes, standards followed)
  3. Examination (chronological, what was done to each item)
  4. Findings (facts; screenshots with hashes where key)
  5. Encryption statement (what was/wasn't accessible, how)
  6. Opinion (labeled as such, within expertise)
  7. Limitations (what you could not determine — honestly)
example.walkthrough: Draft a one-page mock report section 5 (encryption statement) for a BitLocker laptop accessed via escrow key. Honest limits, stated plainly — that is the professional standard.

pitfalls: Jargon without translation — 'we parsed the MFT' means nothing to a jury; explain or lose them.
Hiding limitations — overstated certainty collapses under cross-examination; disclosed limits build trust.
Mixing fact and opinion — unlabeled opinion presented as fact is the fastest way to lose expert status.
lessons.try_it: Write the encryption statement (section 5) for a hypothetical case: LUKS laptop, key recovered from RAM capture. Three paragraphs: what, how, limits.

lessons.title: Escrow Architecture: Where Keys Live
concepts: Key escrow is the enterprise answer to 'what if the user forgets': recovery keys stored in a managed system — Active Directory, cloud MDM, or a dedicated vault — retrievable under policy.
The three-layer model: endpoint generates the key, a transport channel moves it securely at provisioning time, and the escrow store holds it with access controls, audit logging, and backup.
Choose the store by fleet reality: AD-integrated for domain-joined Windows, MDM/cloud escrow for remote and mixed fleets, dedicated vaults (HSM-backed) for regulated or high-risk environments.

The escrow system is now critical infrastructure: if it goes down, recovery stops; if it is breached, every disk is readable. Design its availability and security like production, not like an afterthought.

example.code:
ESCROW ARCHITECTURE
  Endpoint: key generated at provisioning (TPM-sealed where possible)
  Transport: TLS-secured channel, at enrollment only, no retries in cleartext
  Store: AD / MDM / HSM vault — access-controlled, logged, backed up
  Retrieval: role-based, approval workflow, every access audited
  The store's SLA = your recovery SLA. Design accordingly.
example.walkthrough: Inventory where your recovery keys live today and who can read them. If the answer is 'a spreadsheet' or 'I don't know,' the architecture project starts this quarter.

pitfalls: Escrow as an afterthought — bolted-on key storage becomes the weakest link in the encryption story.
Single store, no backup — escrow outage during a recovery wave is a company-stopping event.
Over-broad read access — everyone in IT reading every key is not escrow, it is exposure.
lessons.try_it: Draw your current (or planned) escrow architecture as the four layers above. Mark the layer you trust least — that is the design review topic.

lessons.title: Recovery Operations at Fleet Scale
concepts: At ten laptops, recovery is a phone call; at ten thousand, it is a pipeline: intake, identity verification, key retrieval, user guidance, ticket closure, audit — each step timed and measured.
Define SLAs by scenario: traveling executive locked out at an airport (minutes), standard PIN reset (hours), bulk recovery after a bad update (dedicated war room). One SLA for all is no SLA.
Staff the math: if 2% of a 10,000-device fleet needs recovery monthly, that is 200 tickets — roughly one full-time analyst. Budget the headcount or build the self-service that replaces it.
Runbooks beat heroes: every recovery path documented step-by-step, tested quarterly, executable by the on-call junior at 3 AM. If only one person knows the process, you do not have a process.

example.code:
RECOVERY PIPELINE
  Intake: ticket with device ID + user identity claim
  Verify: identity proofing per policy (MFA, manager, hardware token)
  Retrieve: key from escrow, logged with ticket + approver
  Guide: user through unlock, confirm access restored
  Close: ticket annotated, metrics updated, anomaly review
  METRICS: volume, mean-time-to-recover, self-service rate, after-hours %
example.walkthrough: Write the runbook for your most common recovery scenario this week — the PIN reset. If it takes more than one page, simplify the process, not the document.

pitfalls: No defined SLAs — 'as soon as possible' is not an operations plan.
Hero-dependent recovery — undocumented tribal knowledge fails at 3 AM and during turnover.
Skipping the metrics — you cannot staff or improve what you do not measure.
lessons.try_it: Estimate your fleet's monthly recovery volume (devices × 2%). Write the staffing or self-service plan that covers it.

lessons.title: Self-Service Recovery That Auditors Accept
concepts: Self-service recovery lets verified users retrieve their own keys through a portal — cutting ticket volume dramatically — but only if identity proofing is stronger than the helpdesk script it replaces.
The proofing stack: primary MFA (authenticator or hardware key), plus a second factor like manager approval or a registered backup channel. Single-factor self-service is a key giveaway.
Every self-service retrieval must log: who, which device, when, from where, and the approval chain. Auditors accept self-service when the logs prove the controls — they reject it when logs are thin.
Abuse controls matter: rate-limit retrievals, alert on anomalous patterns (multiple devices, odd hours, new locations), and require step-up verification for VIP or bulk requests.

example.code:
SELF-SERVICE BLUEPRINT
  Portal: SSO + MFA required, device-bound session
  Proofing: MFA + (manager approval OR hardware-key attestation)
  Retrieval: key displayed once, never emailed; session logged fully
  Guardrails: 3 retrievals/day/user; anomaly alerts to security
  Audit: immutable log — who/what/when/where/approver, retained per policy
example.walkthrough: Evaluate your identity stack against the blueprint: can your MFA and approval workflows support it? The portal is easy; the proofing is the project.

pitfalls: Single-factor self-service — convenience that hands keys to anyone with a password.
Logging as an afterthought — thin logs turn self-service into an audit finding.
No anomaly detection — the attacker's first move is bulk retrieval at 3 AM; alert on it.
lessons.try_it: Draft the proofing flow for one self-service retrieval in your environment. Identify the weakest proofing step and how you would strengthen it.

lessons.title: Auditing Escrow: Proving the Controls Work
concepts: Escrow audits answer three questions: are all keys actually escrowed, is access limited to authorized retrieval, and would we detect misuse? Answer with evidence, not assertions.
Coverage audit: compare the escrow store against the device inventory — every encrypted device should have a retrievable key. The gap list is your remediation backlog.
Access audit: review who retrieved which keys, whether each retrieval had a ticket and approval, and whether dormant privileged accounts still hold read access. Orphaned access is the silent killer.
Report the audit in control language: '98.4% key coverage, 100% of retrievals ticketed, 3 orphaned accounts remediated.' Auditors and boards both speak this dialect.

example.code:
ESCROW AUDIT CHECKLIST (quarterly)
  ☐ Coverage: escrowed keys ÷ encrypted devices (target ≥99%)
  ☐ Retrieval review: 100% of retrievals mapped to tickets + approvals
  ☐ Access review: privileged readers current, orphans removed
  ☐ Store health: backups tested, replication lag checked
  ☐ Anomaly sweep: bulk/odd-hour retrievals investigated
  ☐ Report: metrics + remediations, signed off
example.walkthrough: Run the coverage check this month: escrowed keys versus your device inventory. The gap percentage is the most important number in your escrow program — know it cold.

pitfalls: Auditing the store but not the coverage — a pristine vault missing 15% of keys is a failing program.
Annual-only access reviews — privileged access drifts monthly; review quarterly at least.
Metrics without remediation — a gap list nobody works is just a documented failure.
lessons.try_it: Pull your device inventory count and your escrowed key count. Compute coverage and write the one-paragraph remediation plan for the gap.

lessons.title: Key Rotation and Lifecycle Events
concepts: Rotation replaces keys on a schedule or trigger: time-based (annual), event-based (employee departure, suspected compromise, device transfer), and always after any escrow access anomaly.
The rotation workflow: generate new key, escrow it, activate on endpoint, verify, then destroy the old key — in that order. Destroying before verifying is how you brick a fleet.
Lifecycle events that demand rotation: privileged admin departure, helpdesk compromise, escrow store migration, and any retrieval-log anomaly. Define the triggers in policy before the incident.
Crypto-shredding — destroying the key to destroy the data — makes decommissioning instant and provable: no key, no data, no forensic recovery. Build it into the disposal runbook.

example.code:
ROTATION RUNBOOK
  Trigger: [schedule | departure | compromise | anomaly]
  1. Generate new key (HSM/KMS) → 2. Escrow + verify retrievable
  3. Push to endpoint → 4. Confirm activation (telemetry)
  5. Destroy old key in escrow → 6. Log the full chain
  NEVER: destroy-then-verify. ALWAYS: verify-then-destroy.
  DECOMMISSION: crypto-shred (destroy keys) → verify unrecoverable → release hardware
example.walkthrough: Define your rotation triggers in writing this quarter — schedule plus the four event triggers. An unwritten trigger is a rotation that will not happen when it matters.

pitfalls: Rotation without verification — unconfirmed new keys plus destroyed old keys equals bricked devices.
No event triggers — time-based rotation alone misses every departure and compromise.
Forgetting crypto-shredding — physical destruction is slow and unprovable; key destruction is instant and auditable.
lessons.try_it: Write the rotation trigger list for your environment: schedule plus events. For one trigger (e.g., admin departure), draft the 24-hour action timeline.

lessons.title: Envelope Encryption: The Core Pattern
concepts: Envelope encryption protects data with a data key, then protects the data key with a key-encryption key (KEK) — two layers, so the master key never touches the data and data keys can rotate freely.
The flow: generate a unique data key per object, encrypt the data, encrypt the data key with the KEK, store both the ciphertext and the encrypted data key together. Decryption reverses the envelope.
Why it wins: the KEK lives in the KMS/HSM and never leaves; data keys are cheap and disposable; compromising one data key exposes one object, not the kingdom.
Every major cloud KMS implements this pattern (AWS SSE-KMS, Azure Key Vault, GCP Cloud KMS) — learn the pattern once and the provider specifics are just API shapes.

example.code:
ENVELOPE (encrypt)
  1. data_key = GenerateDataKey()          # unique per object
  2. ciphertext = AES(data, data_key)    # fast, local
  3. sealed_key = KMS.Encrypt(data_key, KEK)  # KEK never leaves KMS
  4. store(ciphertext + sealed_key)
  DECRYPT: KMS.Decrypt(sealed_key) → data_key → AES-decrypt
  ROTATE KEK: re-wrap data keys — data itself untouched ✓
example.walkthrough: Trace one object through the envelope in your head: which key touches the data, which key never leaves the KMS, and what happens to each on rotation? That mental model is the whole pattern.

pitfalls: Encrypting data directly with the master key — one compromise exposes everything; the envelope exists to prevent this.
Storing data keys in plaintext 'temporarily' — the envelope's security collapses to the weakest storage.
Re-encrypting all data on KEK rotation — unnecessary; re-wrapping data keys is the point of the envelope.
lessons.try_it: Write the six-step envelope flow from memory (three encrypt, three decrypt). Then note which step fails if the KMS is unreachable — that is your availability design point.

lessons.title: KMS in Practice: AWS, Azure, GCP
concepts: AWS KMS: customer-managed keys (CMKs) with key policies, automatic annual rotation, and CloudTrail logging of every use. Envelope via GenerateDataKey; never export the CMK plaintext.
Azure Key Vault: keys in vaults (software or HSM-backed Managed HSM), RBAC plus key-level permissions, rotation via automated rotation policies. Disk encryption sets tie VM disks to your keys.
GCP Cloud KMS: key rings holding keys with rotation schedules, IAM-based access, and audit logs. Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) attach to storage, BigQuery, and more.
The universal rules: separate duties (key admins ≠ data admins), log every key use to immutable storage, rotate on schedule and on incident, and test restore — an untested key backup is a hope.

example.code:
KMS HYGIENE (all providers)
  ☐ CMK per sensitivity tier (not one key for everything)
  ☐ Key admins ≠ data admins (separation of duties)
  ☐ Automatic rotation enabled + tested
  ☐ Every key use logged → immutable log store, alerted
  ☐ Break-glass procedure documented + drilled
  ☐ Restore tested: can you decrypt from backup with escrowed keys?
example.walkthrough: Audit one cloud account against the six hygiene rows this week. The most common failure is a single shared key with five admins — segment it before the audit finds it.

pitfalls: One key for everything — blast radius of one, convenience of none when it must rotate.
Key admins who are also data admins — separation of duties exists because collusion is a threat model.
Untested restore — discovering your backup keys do not work during an incident is the worst possible timing.
lessons.try_it: Pick one cloud KMS you use. Write which keys exist, who administers them, and whether rotation is on. Fix the weakest row.

lessons.title: At Rest vs In Transit vs In Use
concepts: At rest in the cloud: encrypted volumes (EBS/SSE), encrypted object storage, encrypted databases — the provider handles the mechanics, you handle the key ownership (CMK vs provider-managed).
In transit: TLS everywhere — between users and services, between services, and to the KMS itself. Cloud networks are shared infrastructure; treat every hop as untrusted.

In use: confidential computing (encrypted memory enclaves), field-level encryption for sensitive columns, and strict IAM so decrypted data reaches only authorized compute. The hardest state, now as then.
The shared-responsibility line: the provider secures the infrastructure; you secure your data, keys, and access. Misreading that line is the root cause of most cloud breaches.

example.code:
CLOUD THREE-STATES MAP
  REST:    EBS/SSE-S3/RDS encryption + CMK ownership + backup encryption
  TRANSIT: TLS 1.2+ all hops; private endpoints; no plaintext protocols
  USE:     confidential VMs/enclaves; column-level encryption; least-privilege IAM
  YOUR SIDE OF THE LINE: keys, IAM, configs, data classification
  THEIR SIDE: physical, hypervisor, network fabric
example.walkthrough: Map one cloud workload across the three states and draw the responsibility line. Every item on your side without an owner is an accepted risk you never actually accepted.

pitfalls: Assuming provider-managed encryption is enough — it protects against disk theft, not against misconfigured IAM or your own access.
Plaintext between services — 'inside the VPC' is not a security boundary; encrypt the hops.
Forgetting backups and snapshots — they inherit nothing automatically; encrypt and key them deliberately.
lessons.try_it: Choose one production cloud workload. List its rest/transit/use controls and mark which side of the shared-responsibility line each sits on.

lessons.title: Key Hierarchy: From Root Key to Data Key
concepts: A key hierarchy layers trust: a root/master key (in HSM, rarely used) wraps KEKs, which wrap data keys, which encrypt data. Compromise at a lower layer is contained; the root stays safe.

Depth buys containment: rotating a data key is cheap and frequent; rotating a KEK re-wraps without touching data; rotating the root is rare, planned, and ceremonial — each layer rotates at its own cadence.

Limit the root's exposure: it should never leave the HSM, be used only for wrapping, and require multi-party ceremony (two custodians, audited) for any operation. Convenience at the root is compromise.
Document the hierarchy as a diagram with owners per layer: who can rotate the KEK, who approves root ceremony, what triggers each rotation. Undocumented hierarchy is unmanageable hierarchy.

example.code:
HIERARCHY
  ROOT (HSM, offline-capable) — wraps KEKs; ceremony-only access
    └─ KEK per tier/app — wraps data keys; annual rotation
         └─ DATA KEY per object/volume — encrypts data; frequent rotation
  RULES: lower layers never see upper plaintext; rotation cascades down,
         never up; every layer has a named owner + rotation trigger
example.walkthrough: Diagram your current key hierarchy (or the absence of one). If everything is one key, you have a hierarchy of depth one — the diagram will make the risk visceral.

pitfalls: Flat keying — one key for all data turns every rotation into a crisis and every compromise into a catastrophe.
Root key in software — a root that leaves the HSM is a root waiting to be copied.
No rotation triggers per layer — 'rotate annually' without owners and triggers is a wish, not a control.
lessons.try_it: Draw a three-layer hierarchy for a hypothetical app (web tier + database + backups). Assign an owner and rotation trigger to each layer.

lessons.title: Compliance Mapping for Cloud Encryption
concepts: Compliance frameworks do not ask 'are you encrypted' — they ask which controls, managed how, evidenced where: map each requirement to your specific implementation and its proof.

The common mappings: PCI DSS (cardholder data encrypted at rest/in transit, key management procedures), HIPAA (encryption addressable but effectively required, audit controls), SOC 2 (encryption as part of CC6 logical access), FedRAMP/CMMC (FIPS 140-2 validated modules).
Evidence is the deliverable: KMS key policies, rotation logs, CloudTrail/Vault audit exports, architecture diagrams, and the mapping document itself. Auditors collect artifacts, not assurances.
Crypto-agility is the emerging requirement: document which algorithms you use where, so post-quantum migration is a project plan, not an archaeology expedition.

example.code:
MAPPING TABLE (example row)
  Requirement: PCI DSS 3.4 — PAN encrypted at rest
  Implementation: RDS + S3 with CMEK (CMK: prod-pci-01), envelope pattern
  Key mgmt: annual rotation, dual-control root, CloudTrail logging
  Evidence: key policy export, rotation log, architecture diagram §4.2
  Owner: [name]  Last validated: [date]  Next review: [date]
example.walkthrough: Build one mapping row for your most regulated workload this week. The discipline of one complete row — requirement to evidence — is the template for the whole program.

pitfalls: 'We use AES-256' as the whole answer — auditors need key management, not just algorithms.
Stale mappings — architecture drifted but the document did not; revalidate quarterly.
No algorithm inventory — post-quantum planning starts with knowing what you run where.
lessons.try_it: Write the mapping row for one real requirement your org faces. Identify the evidence artifact you do not have — that is the gap to close.

lessons.title: The Lost Device Playbook
concepts: A lost device is a race between two clocks: the finder/thief's opportunity window and your response time. The playbook's job is to make your clock faster — every step pre-decided, no meetings required.

Minute-zero actions: confirm encryption status from management telemetry, attempt location, lock the device remotely, and open the incident ticket with device ID, user, data classification, and last-seen time.

The encryption verdict determines the incident class: verified FDE with strong auth = low-risk equipment loss; unverified or weak = potential breach with notification obligations. Verify, don't assume.
Communicate on a need-to-know cadence: user, manager, security, and (if breach-class) legal/PR — each with the facts they need, none with speculation. Rumor fills every information vacuum.

example.code:
LOST DEVICE PLAYBOOK (first 60 minutes)
  0-10m:  Confirm encryption status (telemetry) + open ticket
  10-20m: Remote lock + locate attempt; notify user + manager
  20-40m: Classify: verified-FDE (equipment loss) vs unverified (breach?)
  40-60m: If breach-class → engage legal, preserve logs, start timeline
  AFTER:  recovery or wipe decision, lessons-learned, playbook update
  The whole first hour runs from this card — no improvisation.
example.walkthrough: Print the 60-minute card and tape it inside the SOC runbook today. Then tabletop it once: the team that has rehearsed the hour performs it; the team that hasn't invents it under stress.

pitfalls: Improvising the first hour — every lost device becomes a custom incident without a playbook.
Assuming encryption — 'it should be encrypted' is not a telemetry reading; verify from management data.
Over-communicating speculation — early guesses become permanent record; share facts, mark unknowns.
lessons.try_it: Walk through the 60-minute card against your current tooling: which steps can you actually execute today? Fix the first gap.

lessons.title: Theft Response: The First 24 Hours
concepts: Theft differs from loss: assume adversarial intent. The device is now in hostile hands, and your timeline must beat theirs — lock and locate immediately, wipe decision within hours not days.

Evidence preservation runs parallel to containment: snapshot management logs, authentication records, and network telemetry before they age out — you may need to prove what the thief could and could not access.

The wipe decision balances data destruction against evidence and recovery: wiping kills the thief's access but also kills locate/tracking and any forensic value. Decide by data classification, pre-defined in policy.
File the police report with serials and identifiers — it is both a recovery avenue and a compliance artifact. 'We didn't report it' reads terribly in every post-incident review.

example.code:
THEFT 24-HOUR TIMELINE
  H0:   Lock + locate; ticket; confirm encryption telemetry
  H1:   Preserve logs (auth, MDM, network); notify security lead
  H2-4: Wipe decision per data-classification policy; execute if warranted
  H4-8: Police report filed; user/manager/legal notified per class
  H24:  Incident review scheduled; monitoring for device reappearance
  PARALLEL: evidence preservation never waits for containment decisions
example.walkthrough: Check your MDM today: can you lock, locate, and wipe from one console in under five minutes? If any action needs a ticket to another team, the 24-hour timeline is fiction.

pitfalls: Treating theft like loss — adversarial intent changes the clock and the decisions.
Wiping before preserving logs — containment that destroys your own evidence.
Skipping the police report — it costs an hour and pays in recovery odds and compliance posture.
lessons.try_it: Time yourself executing lock + locate in your MDM console (test device). If it takes more than five minutes, streamline the access path.

lessons.title: Legal Hold vs Remote Wipe
concepts: Legal hold freezes data: when litigation is reasonably anticipated, relevant devices must be preserved — wiping a held device is spoliation, with sanctions that dwarf the incident.
Remote wipe destroys data: the right call for high-classification data on an unrecoverable device — the wrong call when a hold exists or when the device may be recovered with evidence intact.
The conflict protocol: the moment legal anticipates litigation, security's wipe authority suspends for held devices — and this must be a pre-agreed, written protocol, not a hallway argument at 2 AM.
Document the decision either way: wipe or hold, who decided, on what authority, at what time. The post-incident question is never just 'what did you do' — it is 'show me you decided properly.'

example.code:
HOLD vs WIPE DECISION
  Legal hold active? → HOLD. No wipe. Preserve. (spoliation risk)
  No hold + high-classification data + unrecoverable → WIPE
  No hold + low-classification + recovery plausible → LOCK + TRACK
  Authority: [named role] decides; legal consulted within [X] hours
  Record: decision, authority, time, rationale — in the ticket
example.walkthrough: Get the hold-vs-wipe protocol signed by legal and security leadership this quarter. The 2 AM version of this argument, without a written protocol, is how companies earn sanctions.

pitfalls: Wiping under hold — spoliation sanctions exceed almost any breach cost.
No pre-agreed protocol — incident-time authority disputes paralyze both teams.
Undocumented decisions — proper calls without records still fail the review.
lessons.try_it: Draft the one-page hold-vs-wipe protocol for your org: triggers, authority, and the documentation requirement. Get legal's initials on it.

lessons.title: Verifying Encryption Posture After an Incident
concepts: After any device incident, verify the fleet — not just the device: pull encryption compliance telemetry for the whole population and confirm the lost device was actually representative, not an exception.

The three verification questions: was the device encrypted (telemetry proof), was the key escrowed (retrieval test), and was the auth strong (policy compliance)? Answer all three from data, not memory.
Treat every incident as a sampling audit: check ten random devices' encryption, escrow, and auth posture. Incidents reveal systemic gaps more often than individual failures.
Close the loop publicly: share the verified findings and the fixes with the org. 'We checked 10,000 devices and fixed 140' builds more trust than 'the incident is resolved.'

example.code:
POST-INCIDENT VERIFICATION
  1. Device: encryption telemetry + escrow retrieval test + auth policy check
  2. Fleet sample: 10 random devices, same three checks
  3. Gaps: remediate (re-encrypt, re-escrow, re-enroll) with deadlines
  4. Report: findings + fixes, shared with stakeholders
  5. Playbook: update the card with what this incident taught
example.walkthrough: Run the fleet-sample check this month as a drill — ten random devices, three checks each. The gaps you find in peacetime are free; the ones incidents find are expensive.

pitfalls: Verifying only the incident device — the fleet is the population; the device was a sample.
Trusting policy over telemetry — 'should be encrypted' lost to 'was encrypted' in every incident review.
Skipping the public close-out — silent fixes teach the org nothing; shared findings prevent repeats.
lessons.try_it: Pull encryption telemetry for ten random devices in your fleet today. Record the compliance rate — that number is your real posture.

lessons.title: Executive and VIP Device Protection
concepts: Executives are high-value targets with low security patience: their devices need stronger protection delivered with less friction — the standard fleet policy, executed flawlessly, plus targeted extras.

The VIP baseline: verified FDE, hardware-key MFA, shortest auto-lock the executive will tolerate, travel-mode protocols (loaner devices for high-risk destinations), and a dedicated 24/7 recovery path.

Travel is the threat window: border crossings, hotel networks, and device separation (theft/loss/confiscation). Brief executives before high-risk travel — most incidents are preventable with a 10-minute briefing.

The recovery SLA for VIPs is minutes, not hours: pre-staged verification, named responders, and practiced handoffs. Test it quarterly — the first real VIP incident is not the time to discover the process.

example.code:
VIP PROTECTION PACKAGE
  Device: FDE verified + hardware-key MFA + MDM enrolled + auto-lock ≤2min
  Travel: pre-trip briefing; loaner device option; encrypted backups before departure
  Response: named 24/7 responder; 15-min recovery SLA; executive comms plan
  Review: quarterly posture check + annual travel-threat briefing
  Rule: stronger controls, less friction — never the reverse
example.walkthrough: Identify your VIP population and check each against the package baseline this quarter. The gap between 'executive device' and 'protected executive device' is usually one briefing and one configuration push.

pitfalls: Weaker controls for VIPs 'for convenience' — the highest-value targets with the weakest protection is the worst trade in security.
No travel protocol — border and hotel incidents are predictable; unprepared is a choice.
Untested VIP response — a 15-minute SLA you have never drilled is a hope, not a plan.
lessons.try_it: List your VIP device population. Score each against the five package rows and schedule the quarter's posture checks.

lessons.title: Tabletops: Rehearsing the Worst Day
concepts: Tabletop exercises walk the team through a simulated incident — stolen executive laptop, ransomware on encrypted fleet, escrow outage — with no real systems at risk and every decision examined.
Design for decisions, not theater: injects should force real choices (wipe or hold? notify or contain? who decides?) at the points where your playbook is thinnest.
Include the non-technical players: legal, PR, HR, executives. The incidents that go badly fail at communication and authority, not at technology — rehearse the humans.
Every tabletop ends with action items, owners, and deadlines — and the playbook updated. A tabletop that changes nothing was entertainment, not preparation.

example.code:
TABLETOP DESIGN
  Scenario: [stolen VIP laptop, unencrypted backup found]
  Inject 1 (T+0): device reported stolen, telemetry shows last check-in 6h ago
  Inject 2 (T+30m): thief attempting logins; legal flags possible litigation
  Inject 3 (T+2h): media inquiry arrives; police ask about the device
  DEBRIEF: what did we decide, who decided, what was missing?
  OUTPUT: action items + owners + playbook updates (within 1 week)
example.walkthrough: Schedule one tabletop this quarter using the design above. Invite legal and one executive — their presence transforms it from IT drill to organizational readiness.

pitfalls: Tech-only tabletops — the failures are always communication and authority; rehearse those.
No action items — unrecorded lessons evaporate within a week.
Annual-only cadence — quarterly keeps the playbook alive; annual lets it fossilize.
lessons.try_it: Draft three injects for a tabletop in your environment. Identify who must be in the room for each inject's decision — invite them now.
